four-of-cups.work: Stuck in a role that no longer fits. A new project or opportunity is in the room and you are not seeing it because you are too busy resenting the last one.
four-of-cups.sajuLens: The Four of Cups is 水 (water) energy that has stopped flowing. In saju, 수(水) represents adaptability, depth, the capacity to move through situations without resistance — but the Four shows water that has chosen to be still. For 수(水) Day Masters, this card often reads as a warning about a tendency that is already yours: the ability to be flexible can also become the ability to disappear into circumstances until you forget you had a choice. For 목(木) — wood Day Masters, who naturally push outward and upward, the Four shows something stuck — a frustration with someone who has stopped moving and will not explain why. For 화(火) — fire, the chart's natural actor, the Four appears as a coldness that confuses you. For 금(金) — metal, it reads as a stubbornness you respect until you realize it is just fear. For 토(土) — earth, the grounded element, the Four can feel almost comfortable, which is precisely the problem the card is pointing at.

five-of-cups.title: Five of Cups
five-of-cups.summary: The Five of Cups is sorrow so complete it blinds you to what has not been lost. What it means upright, reversed, and through a saju lens.
meaning: Grief has a way of narrowing vision. The Five of Cups shows someone standing before three spilled cups — the loss is real, the mourning is earned — while two cups remain standing behind them, unnoticed. The card is not arguing that the loss does not matter. It is saying that pain can become so total it rewrites the inventory, makes you forget what survived, turns a partial wound into a complete one. This is the card of sorrow that has calcified into narrative.

There is a bridge visible in the distance, leading toward a fortress, a path that exists whether you are ready to see it or not. The card's quiet argument is that grief requires its own time, but the refusal to look is a choice being made inside that time. The upright Five asks: what are you refusing to count because you are too busy counting what is gone?

symbols.label: The dark sangbok robe
symbols.text: Formal mourning wear in Joseon — not accidental sadness but grief that has been named and dressed for. The figure is not falling apart; they are being held together by protocol. Notice how the structure of the garment mirrors the structure of the emotion: contained, but total.

symbols.label: Three spilled white cups
symbols.text: The cups are porcelain, deliberate, precious — what has broken was real. The spill is complete; nothing is being salvaged. They sit on the ground where they cannot be missed, the visual centre of the card, commanding all attention.

symbols.label: Two upright cups behind
symbols.text: Still standing, still full, still entirely present. The figure's bowed head means they occupy the same space as these cups and do not see them. Loss and survival are occupying the same moment; only attention decides which one is real.

symbols.label: Stone bridge over mist
symbols.text: The path forward exists but is obscured — not gone, not blocked, but difficult to see from where grief is standing. A fortress waits on the other side. The future is drawn but the figure's back is turned to it.

five-of-cups.upright: You are looking at what is broken and calling it the whole story. The loss is real — the card does not dispute that — but your vision has narrowed to fit it. Before you decide that everything is ruined, turn around. Not to pretend the spilled cups do not matter, but to remember what is still standing. The bridge exists. You do not have to cross it today.
five-of-cups.reversed: The refusal to look is loosening. Either you are beginning to notice what has survived, or you are becoming tired enough of the narrative that you are willing to let it shift. The reversal does not erase the loss. It means grief is no longer the only thing in the room.
five-of-cups.love: Loss is real, but so is what remains — if you can stop mourning long enough to see it.
five-of-cups.work: A project or role that has failed, and the failure is complete. Before you close the book entirely, check whether you are grieving the whole thing or just the parts you are looking at.
five-of-cups.sajuLens: The Five of Cups carries 水(water) — emotion, flow, the capacity to hold and release. Upright, it is water that has stopped flowing, become stagnant. For a 수(水) Day Master, this card often reads as a return to native terrain — you understand grief deeply, feel it completely, and the card is asking whether that understanding has become a place to live. For a 화(火) Day Master, the card reads as dampening, as emotion extinguishing the forward momentum fire needs. For 목(木) — wood — it is blockage of growth. The card's reversal suggests water beginning to move again, which reads very differently depending on what element you carry: for water it is healing, for fire it is friction lifting, for wood it is space opening to grow.

six-of-cups.title: Six of Cups
six-of-cups.summary: The Six of Cups holds a moment of pure childhood affection — a boy offering white plum blossoms to a girl in a sunlit Joseon courtyard. What it means upright, reversed, and through a saju lens.
meaning: The Six of Cups is water at rest: emotion that has settled into clarity. It shows up when someone has stopped pretending a feeling is more complicated than it is. A boy offers flowers to a girl. No transaction, no future being negotiated. The white plum blossoms — 매화 — mean exactly what they mean: you are here, this matters, I see you. In Joseon courtyard paintings, this scene marks the moment before the world teaches you to be guarded about warmth.

Nostalgia lives in this card, but not as regret. The older figure walking away in the background is not a threat — it is simply time, moving as it always does. The card asks what happened to your capacity for uncomplicated affection: whether you have outgrown it, whether you have learned to be suspicious of it, or whether it is still there underneath, waiting for permission to show up again.

symbols.label: White plum blossoms in the cup
symbols.text: Not water. Flowers. The offering is beauty itself, with no use-value attached. In Korean tradition 매화 blooms in late winter, marking survival and quiet renewal. Here they say: this is what I have that matters.

symbols.label: Six white cups on stone steps
symbols.text: Arranged around the central exchange, they hold the scene steady. Six is the number of harmony in most traditions — not the breakthrough of five, not the completion of seven, but a moment that feels balanced and whole. These cups are empty and waiting.

symbols.label: Sunlit Joseon courtyard
symbols.text: Soft warm pastels, ivory and blush. The light is not dramatic or testing. It simply illuminates what is already there: two children, flowers, the architecture of a life structured enough to have a place for this moment.

symbols.label: The older figure receding
symbols.text: Walking away in the background, neither watching nor intervening. Adulthood is not hostile in this card — it is simply elsewhere, letting its own childhood live in this one.

six-of-cups.upright: Pure feeling without agenda. Someone is offering you something — attention, loyalty, uncomplicated liking — and the card suggests you are safe enough to accept it without wondering what it costs. This is the warmth of rapport that does not need to justify itself: a moment of recognition between two people where neither is performing. Lean into what is actually being offered instead of editing it into something more acceptable.
six-of-cups.reversed: The affection has either calcified into obligation or been dressed up as something it is not. Reversed, this card warns against mistaking nostalgia for connection, or treating someone's warmth as a debt you must repay. What is being offered may not be as innocent as it appears.
six-of-cups.love: Someone is showing you they like you without conditions attached; the question is whether you can sit with that without ruining it.
six-of-cups.work: A working relationship based on genuine rapport rather than hierarchy. Trust the person across from you more than you trust the formal structure.
six-of-cups.sajuLens: 水 — water governs emotion, memory, and the capacity to receive. For a 水 Day Master, the Six of Cups often reads as a homecoming to your native element — the warmth in this card is how you naturally work. For 火 — fire stems, this gentleness can feel like dampening; fire needs intensity and forward motion, and this card's stillness may register as stalling. A 木 — wood Day Master reads it as nourishment arriving at exactly the right moment. For 金 — metal, the unstructured affection here bypasses all the safety checks; the card asks whether you can afford to lower your guard. 土 — earth finds in it the stable ground where belonging happens.

seven-of-cups.title: Seven of Cups
seven-of-cups.summary: Seven of Cups shows a Joseon nobleman drowning in beautiful options — each cup holds a different dream. The card of choice paralysis, fantasy, and the question of what you actually want.
meaning: Seven cups float in front of you, each one glowing with something desirable: a jade dragon, a golden palace, lotus flowers, a victory banner, a beautiful face, rubies, shadow. The problem is not that none of them are real — the problem is that all of them are equally real inside the dream-mist. This card describes the moment when possibility becomes vertigo. Too many paths that all look true.

The nobleman's gaze moves from cup to cup but does not settle. Water 水 rules emotion and intuition, but seven of them together create a fog rather than clarity. The card is not saying the visions are lies. It is saying that without a way to choose, abundance becomes its own kind of poverty. You are paralyzed not by scarcity but by having to pick.

symbols.label: Seven floating white cups
symbols.text: Each cup contains a different vision — dragon, palace, lotus, banner, face, rubies, shadow. The whiteness makes them all equally bright, equally tempting. None stands out as more real than the others.

symbols.label: The deep indigo dream-mist
symbols.text: The cups do not sit on a table. They hang suspended in cloud. This is the landscape of sleep and fantasy, where the usual rules of weight and consequence do not apply. Nothing here has to land.

symbols.label: The nobleman's divided attention
symbols.text: His eyes cannot rest on one cup. The moment of choice has already become a moment of non-choice — each second spent looking is a second not decided.

symbols.label: The shadow in the seventh cup
symbols.text: Not all visions are bright. One cup holds darkness. The card includes this to say: even knowing one option is hollow does not always help. You can still want it.

seven-of-cups.upright: You are looking at options without yet knowing what you are actually choosing for. The seven cups can represent fantasy — the belief that one of them will solve everything — or simply overload: too many real possibilities at once, each one calling for a different answer. Before you pick, get quiet enough to notice which cup you reach for first, before your thinking mind arrived.
seven-of-cups.reversed: The fog has lifted or is about to. Reversed, this card often marks the moment when one of the visions fails, or when you suddenly see which cup matters. It can also show someone waking up from fantasy and discovering that the real choice is smaller, stranger, or less glamorous than any of the seven.
seven-of-cups.love: Infatuation vs. love: one is a cup you gaze at; the other is the one you actually drink from.
seven-of-cups.work: Too many opportunities and no clear signal about which one fits. Get your criteria straight before you audition the next option.
seven-of-cups.sajuLens: Water 水 rules this card, and water people are naturally drawn to multiple possibilities at once — they see the many paths because they can imagine living inside each one. For a 水 Day Master, Seven of Cups often reads as a return to known terrain: yes, this is what your mind does, and sometimes it paralyzes you. For 火 (fire) Day Masters, who burn forward toward a single target, this card tends to arrive as external chaos rather than internal pattern — the fog is coming from outside, and your job is to cut through it. 木 (wood) Day Masters see it as a growth problem solved by eliminating all but the best root. 金 (metal) Day Masters experience it as noise: too many voices before you have finished listening to the right one. 土 (earth) Day Masters quiet the cups altogether, waiting until one cup calls them directly.

eight-of-cups.title: Eight of Cups
eight-of-cups.summary: The Eight of Cups shows a solitary traveller leaving behind settled feelings to climb toward something deeper. What it means upright, reversed, and through a saju lens.
meaning: Eight cups stand upright in an incomplete row — the work of building something, left behind. The traveller in a Joseon cloak does not look back at what was constructed. Instead he climbs a steep rocky path toward a distant red moon, walking staff in hand, moving from what was comfortable into what calls to him. The card describes the moment when settled satisfaction stops being enough, when the shape you built no longer fits what you have become.

This is not flight from disaster. The cups are whole and arranged. What is being abandoned is functioning — but functionality and meaning are not the same thing. The Eight of Cups marks the threshold where someone stops defending yesterday's choices and admits the next stage is elsewhere. The muted blues and greys of the mountain path suggest this is not a happy decision, only an honest one.

symbols.label: Eight white porcelain cups in an incomplete row
symbols.text: Eight suggests abundance, rhythm, near-completion — but the row is unfinished. What was built works, but it does not feel whole. The white porcelain is Joseon craft, dignified and durable. The traveller is not rejecting quality; he is outgrowing containment.

symbols.label: The cloaked traveller with walking staff
symbols.text: He carries only what moves with him. His posture is already committed to the climb — weight forward, not lingering. The cloak and staff mark him as someone accustomed to journeys, someone for whom leaving is a known language.

symbols.label: The steep rocky mountain path
symbols.text: Steep means deliberate effort ahead. Rocky means unsmoothed terrain, no established route. The path itself is not inviting — this is not an escape into ease, but a conscious choice to trade comfort for something harder and less certain.

symbols.label: The distant red moon
symbols.text: Red carries urgency and depth in Korean visual language. Distant means it cannot yet be reached, only recognized as real. The moon pulls the traveller forward into darkness that is not yet familiar.

eight-of-cups.upright: You have outgrown something that still functions. The next stage is not here; it is ahead, and the path up to it is steep. Leave what you built with respect — it served its purpose — but do not mistake loyalty to the past for loyalty to yourself. The card reads as permission to stop defending a choice simply because you made it.
eight-of-cups.reversed: The cups are being abandoned out of restlessness rather than readiness, or the traveller has climbed halfway and turned back because the path was harder than the view suggested. Ask whether you are moving toward something or only running from something. Real leaving requires clarity about direction, not just exhaustion with where you are.
eight-of-cups.love: A relationship that was stable has stopped being enough — yours or theirs.
eight-of-cups.work: You have mastered this role and the mastery feels like confinement. The next opportunity is elsewhere and smaller on the surface than what you are leaving.
eight-of-cups.sajuLens: 水 — water flows, but it also pools. The Eight of Cups names the moment when a 수 (water) Day Master realizes the pool has become stagnant. For water types, this card often reads as necessity rather than choice — the system that was working has calcified, and movement is the only path forward. For 금 (metal) Day Masters, the card warns against confusing stability with success; metal prizes order and completion, so leaving what is functionally complete can feel like failure rather than evolution. For 목 (wood) types, the climb is natural — growth always moves toward new territory. 火 (fire) Day Masters may find the solitary mountain path unsatisfying; fire needs audience and warmth, but this journey offers only discipline and distance.

nine-of-cups.title: Nine of Cups
nine-of-cups.summary: The Nine of Cups is wish-fulfillment made visible — the moment when effort stops being abstract and becomes a room you can sit in. What it means upright, reversed, and through a saju lens.
meaning: The Nine of Cups arrives when a want has finished its work and turned into something tangible. In the KSaju deck it is a Joseon merchant at rest on a low bench, arms crossed, the kind of settled satisfaction that does not need to perform itself. Behind him nine white porcelain cups sit on curved shelves — the exact number he wished for, the exact form he imagined. The card is not about the wishing; it is about the quiet moment after, when you can finally stop reaching.

This is material success without apology, and without the strain of still pursuing it. Water 水 (the element of cups) naturally moves toward collecting, pooling, finding its level — and here it has found it. The merchant is not restraining himself or preparing for loss. He is simply sitting with what arrived. The card asks: can you let yourself have this without immediately looking past it?

symbols.label: Nine white porcelain cups on curved shelves
symbols.text: Porcelain was luxury in Joseon — refined, fragile, deliberate. They are displayed, not hidden, which means the fulfillment is part of the pleasure. The number nine completes the suit before the final card arrives. What was wished for has arrived exactly.

symbols.label: The merchant's crossed arms and deep smile
symbols.text: Not the smile of someone still working, but of someone who has stopped and found the stopping good. The posture is at rest, stable, closed around its own contentment. There is no hunger left in this image.

symbols.label: Warm golden candlelight and deep blue curtains
symbols.text: The gold speaks to prosperity and the deliberate lighting of a private space. The blue frames it without darkening it — this is fulfillment in a contained, protected sphere, warm and held.

symbols.label: The low wooden bench
symbols.text: Not grand furniture but solid, grounded, the kind made for staying. It suggests a man who has settled into his own life rather than performing it.

nine-of-cups.upright: This card is permission to stop climbing. The thing you reached for is here, visible, real — the nine cups are not metaphorical. Sit with it for a moment before the next want pulls at you. The Nine of Cups is not cautioning you against loss; it is asking whether you can taste what you already have, whether you can let satisfaction be complete instead of treating it as a platform for the next hunger.
nine-of-cups.reversed: Either the cups remain on the shelf, seen but untouched, or you are sitting with them while your attention is elsewhere — already planning the next ascent. Reversed, the card often points to fulfillment that arrives but cannot be received, either because it does not match the picture you held, or because you have already moved past wanting it.
nine-of-cups.love: The wish fulfills, but watch whether you are grateful for this person or grateful to have stopped searching.
nine-of-cups.work: A goal closes. Let yourself acknowledge it before the habit of striving pulls you toward the next one.
nine-of-cups.sajuLens: Water 水 naturally gathers and collects; the Nine of Cups shows that gathering complete. For a 水 (water) Day Master, this card often reads simply as home — the element doing what it does. For 火 (fire) Day Masters, whose nature is to burn through and move on, the card can feel static or even trapping; fulfillment reads less like rest and more like being held in place. For 木 (wood) Day Masters, expansion-driven, the nine cups may feel like a final inventory rather than an opening. For 金 (metal) Day Masters, the formed and finished satisfies; this card often lands well. For 土 (earth) Day Masters, the stability resonates, though earth tends to feel deserving of more.

ten-of-cups.title: Ten of Cups
ten-of-cups.summary: The Ten of Cups is fulfillment that does not need to be earned or proved — happiness in ordinary time, built from small gestures and shared air.
meaning: The Ten of Cups does not arrive as a prize. It arrives as a day. The card shows a Joseon family before their tile-roofed home, the parents embracing and looking upward together while the children dance with open arms, and above them a rainbow arc of ten glowing white porcelain cups — not distant, not symbolic, but present and close enough to see clearly. This is contentment that has moved into daily life and stopped feeling temporary.

What makes the card work is its refusal to dramatize itself. There is no struggle visible, no obstacle overcome, no moment of recognition or turning point. The mountains and river sit quietly in the background. The happiness here is sustained by a kind of gentleness: people at ease with one another, able to look upward together without needing anything to change. The card suggests that this is what permanence actually feels like — not fixed, but repeated, not forced, but chosen again each morning.

symbols.label: The rainbow arc of ten white cups
symbols.text: They glow above the family's heads, visible and real but unthreatening. Ten represents completion, but these cups do not feel distant or aspirational — they are the abundance of daily life made visible, close enough to understand, simple enough to repeat.

symbols.label: The embrace between the parents
symbols.text: They hold each other while looking upward together. The posture shows agreement without need for words, comfort without demand. This is partnership that has stopped performing and started living.

symbols.label: The children dancing with arms open
symbols.text: Their movement is unguarded and unselfconscious, arising from the atmosphere around them rather than from effort. They are free not because they have been given permission but because they are held inside something that feels stable.

symbols.label: The tile-roofed home and the river
symbols.text: Traditional, settled, and surrounded by landscape that does not ask for anything. The home is where this contentment lives; it is built into the structure of daily return.

ten-of-cups.upright: Happiness that does not announce itself or require justification. The card points to relationships that have earned their ease through time and small repeated kindnesses, to a home that feels like home rather than like an achievement, to contentment that is so ordinary it is easy to miss. This is the card of people who have stopped waiting for permission to be satisfied with what they have already built. Notice that no one is reaching for anything.
ten-of-cups.reversed: The happiness is being forced or performed, held together by obligation rather than by genuine ease. Reversed, the card points to a family held together by what it looks like from outside, or to contentment that requires constant work to maintain. Check whether you are still choosing this, or whether you are simply continuing it.
ten-of-cups.love: Relationship that has stopped being a project and become a home — the kind that asks for nothing except to be lived in.
ten-of-cups.work: A workplace or role where you belong. You have moved past the need to prove yourself here, and that shift is visible.
ten-of-cups.sajuLens: Water — 水 — governs flow and connection; it is the element of relationships, receptivity, the bonds that hold a family together. In saju terms, the Ten of Cups reads as the 水(water) moment made stable: relationships have settled into their final form. For a water 일간 (Day Master), this card often shows what you are building toward — the peace that comes from being needed and accepted exactly as you are. For a 火(fire) Day Master, the card may read as a destination that requires you to stop moving toward it: in saju terms, fire cannot rest in water, and this card asks whether you can be content with something that does not demand your constant attention or transformation.

page-of-cups.title: Page of Cups
page-of-cups.summary: The Page of Cups is curiosity without agenda — a young scholar notices a fish that has learned to speak. What it means upright, reversed, and through a saju lens.
meaning: The Page of Cups is the card of noticing something that does not fit the ordinary world and being delighted rather than skeptical. In the KSaju deck he is a Joseon scholar-boy in blue and silver, standing at the shoreline where land stops being practical — a place where a fish can jump from a cup and speak, and he does not question it. This is what 水 — water does: it receives, it makes space, it lets the strange thing happen without first running the numbers on whether it is sensible.

The card describes an open mind, but not in an abstract way. It is the mind that still finds things surprising. His wonder is not performed — it is the condition he is in when something impossible arrives and he has not yet learned the reasons to refuse it. When this card turns up it usually means you have noticed something worth following, even though you cannot yet see where it leads or why you should trust it.

symbols.label: The blue fish speaking from the cup
symbols.text: A creature that should not be able to leave the porcelain has done so, and is speaking. This is the card's whole argument: the thing you were not looking for has arrived anyway, and it is trying to get your attention. The cup is ordinary; the fish is not.

symbols.label: His delighted surprise
symbols.text: His expression is open, not guarded. He is young enough — or open enough — that seeing something impossible has not yet taught him to close down. The emotion is genuine and without calculation. This is what curiosity looks like before it learns strategy.

symbols.label: The single wave behind him
symbols.text: Water in motion, but gentle. There is movement and change here, but nothing violent. The 水 — water element moves him toward new feeling without force, the way waves work when no one is fighting them.

symbols.label: Aquamarine and silver light
symbols.text: The colours are dreamlike and soft. This is the card of imagination not yet constrained by what others have told you is real. The light does not clarify; it deepens the mystery.

page-of-cups.upright: You have noticed something that matters, even though it has no practical justification yet. Let yourself be curious about it without immediately asking whether it is sensible. This card favours the beginner exactly because he has not yet been trained to dismiss what does not fit the categories he knows. Follow the small strange thing. The significance will become clear only after you have already decided to pay attention.
page-of-cups.reversed: The imagination is there but the courage to follow it is not. Reversed, this card often points to an idea or a feeling you have already talked yourself out of before giving it real time. You saw the fish; you just decided it was not real. Check whether you are being prudent or whether you are simply afraid of looking foolish.
page-of-cups.love: A feeling you did not plan for has arrived. Let it speak before you decide whether it is impossible.
page-of-cups.work: An idea that does not yet fit the existing categories. It is worth taking seriously precisely because you cannot immediately sort it into what you already know.
page-of-cups.sajuLens: The Page of Cups runs on 水 — water: receptivity, imagination, the willingness to be moved by what you have not anticipated. If your 일간 is a water stem, this card usually reads as recognition — you are already operating in this mode. If your Day Master is 火 — fire, which moves toward clarity and distinction, the Page can feel almost uncomfortably vague; what it is inviting you toward is the opposite of the sharp edges fire prefers. If you are 金 — metal, the card points to what gets lost when you filter reality through structure too early: this one is asking you to stay curious a little longer before sorting.

knight-of-cups.title: Knight of Cups
knight-of-cups.summary: The Knight of Cups approaches with feeling held steady. A Joseon nobleman on horseback, offering a porcelain cup. What it means upright, reversed, and through a saju lens.
meaning: The Knight of Cups is water moving with deliberation. He is not the wild flood or the still pond — he is the stream that knows exactly where it is going and arrives without splashing. In the KSaju deck he wears the formal bearing of a Joseon nobleman, his robe embroidered with fish and waves, mounted on a white horse and moving forward with purpose. The cup he extends is an offering made calmly, not desperately. This is what emotional maturity looks like: feeling strong enough to share without needing it back immediately.

The card suggests a moment where emotion and action are no longer at odds. Someone (or some part of yourself) is approaching with grace. There is no uncertainty in his posture, no apology in the gesture — only a clear intention to connect. When the Knight of Cups appears, it usually means that what is coming has already been decided in the heart. The only question left is whether you are ready to receive it.

symbols.label: Blue and silver robe with fish and wave embroidery
symbols.text: The water is not worn as decoration but as identity. Fish and waves are the language he speaks. This is someone at home in the element of emotion, fluent in it, not fighting it or pretending it is not there.

symbols.label: White porcelain cup extended forward
symbols.text: Porcelain is formal, precious, intentional — this is not an impulse but an offering prepared in advance. The cup is held steady and extended, not thrust or withheld. It is already decided that he will give it; the only moment left is the giving.

symbols.label: Helmet with silver wings
symbols.text: Even in armor there is grace. The winged helmet suggests movement that is both grounded and able to rise — emotion that is guided but not trapped, contained but not suffocated.

symbols.label: White horse and misty mountain lake
symbols.text: The white horse is pure motion without resistance. The misty lake behind him is the emotional territory he has already crossed, visible but softened by distance. He is not bringing the past drama with him.

knight-of-cups.upright: Someone or something is arriving with emotional clarity and steady intention. The Knight of Cups does not doubt what he feels — he has simply learned to move it forward without letting it scatter. If this is about a person, they are showing up the way they mean to. If it is about your own impulse, trust that the steadiness is real. Receive what is being offered, and notice that it comes without pressure attached.
knight-of-cups.reversed: The graceful bearing has cracked. Either the emotion is there but the clarity is gone — all feeling and no direction — or the steadiness was only performance, and it is finally showing the strain. Someone may be offering what they cannot actually give. Check whether what is approaching is genuine or whether it is an echo of what you wanted to hear.
knight-of-cups.love: A romantic approach that has thought itself through. Someone knows what they want and is calm enough to let you decide.
knight-of-cups.work: A proposal or a new role presented with both competence and consideration. This person or opportunity arrives without drama.
knight-of-cups.sajuLens: The Knight of Cups is 水 (water) in motion — emotion given form and direction. For a 수(水) Day Master, this card often reads as recognition: you are being seen the way you actually move. For 화(火) — fire Day Masters, who tend toward intensity and urgency, the Knight's unhurried approach can feel frustratingly slow, yet it often points to a connection that will outlast the moment because it is not burning itself up. For 토(土) — earth, which needs stability, the Knight's grace is reassuring: emotion that has learned to hold its shape. 목(木) — wood Day Masters may read this card as a call to patience; the growth is real but it is not going to rush. 금(金) — metal reads it as precision applied to feeling: emotion made disciplined and therefore trustworthy.

queen-of-cups.title: Queen of Cups
queen-of-cups.summary: The Queen of Cups holds the secrets of the heart with an open hand. Emotional wisdom, artistic depth, and the capacity to feel without drowning.
meaning: She sits at the water's edge in full ceremonial dress, feet touching the surface she has mastered. The covered cup she holds is not locked away — it is simply kept with intention. This is the card of someone who has learned that depth and composure are not opposites: you can feel everything and still hold the line. Her empathy is not a weakness that overwhelms her; it is a skill she has developed to the point where it becomes invisible, like breathing.

The Queen of Cups is the artist, the counselor, the person who can sit with another's sorrow without flinching or trying to fix it. She knows that some things are not meant to be solved but held. Her throne is made from coral and shell — the hard structures built by soft creatures — which is exactly what she is. She has boundaries because she understands how necessary they are for anyone who feels this much.

symbols.label: The ornate covered cup
symbols.text: What it holds remains unseen, but the intensity of her gaze suggests she knows exactly what it is. This is emotional knowledge kept private — not hidden, but protected. Some secrets are meant to be guarded, not broadcast.

symbols.label: The coral and shell throne
symbols.text: Hard structures built by vulnerable creatures. She has constructed something solid from sensitivity. The throne sits at the water's edge, neither fully in the sea nor entirely on land — she moves between worlds.

symbols.label: Teal and blue daeryebok
symbols.text: The ceremonial dress is water-coloured and deliberately chosen. She has claimed her role. This is not an accident of birth but a mastered identity — the queen who knows exactly what she is.

symbols.label: Feet touching the water
symbols.text: She is not afraid of the element she governs. Contact is maintained, gentle and direct. This is the card of someone at home in her own depths.

queen-of-cups.upright: Emotional maturity and artistic sensitivity. You can feel what others feel without losing yourself in it. The card asks you to trust your intuition, to create from what you know, and to let others rest in your presence without needing to be fixed. Your capacity for depth is not a burden — it is your instrument.
queen-of-cups.reversed: Feeling overwhelmed, or using sensitivity as a screen for avoidance. The reversed Queen lets emotion dictate action, drowns in other people's problems, or keeps her own feelings so carefully locked that nothing genuine moves. Check whether you are protecting yourself or hiding.
queen-of-cups.love: Someone who understands you without needing explanation — or a reminder to become that person.
queen-of-cups.work: An artist, counselor, or anyone who trades in emotional attunement. Your job requires you to feel accurately and stay clear-headed. That combination is rare.
queen-of-cups.sajuLens: The Queen of Cups runs on 水(water) — the element of flow, depth, and the capacity to receive and hold. If your 일간 is a water stem, this card describes how you already operate: feeling first, understanding later, moving with circumstance rather than against it. For 火(fire) Day Masters, this Queen often reads as unfamiliar — the card is asking you to sit still instead of act, to listen instead of speak. For 土(earth) natives, she can feel like she lacks structure; you may need to trust her method even when you cannot see the framework. 金(metal) Day Masters see her as scattered unless they remember that her precision operates in the emotional register, not the material one. 木(wood) finds in her a kindred depth, though wood moves faster than water does.

king-of-cups.title: King of Cups
king-of-cups.summary: The King of Cups masters emotion through intellect and experience. What it means upright, reversed, and through a saju lens.
meaning: The King of Cups is the court card that has already passed through the emotional storms the other cups depict. He sits on stone, not wood — his throne is unmovable — while the sea around him churns. The white cup he holds is not trembling. This is not numbness or detachment; it is the skill of someone who has felt deeply enough and long enough to know which feelings matter and which are weather. He has learned to think with the heart instead of being thought by it.

The lotus scepter marks this as wisdom earned through practice, not principle. In Joseon court symbolism the lotus rises from mud untouched — it represents emergence into clarity. The fish leaping at his side is the only restless thing in the frame, and even that small motion does not disturb his attention. This king knows that mastery is not the absence of feeling. It is the presence of something larger that feeling can move through without breaking.

symbols.label: The stone throne
symbols.text: Stone does not bend or absorb. It stays itself regardless of what crashes against it. The throne says this king's groundedness is not passive — it is a chosen position held against the weight of everything trying to move him.

symbols.label: The white cup
symbols.text: White holds all colours or none, depending on how you look at it. The cup is held steadily, neither hidden nor offered. This is containment by choice, not by force.

symbols.label: Deep blue and gold robe with fish embroidery
symbols.text: Gold does not rust in salt water. The fish moving through the weave are part of the fabric itself — the king does not separate from the emotional realm but has woven it into his own being.

symbols.label: The turbulent sea
symbols.text: The chaos is real and it is directly beside him. The card does not promise calm conditions. It shows a man who remains steady inside them.

king-of-cups.upright: This is the card of someone thinking clearly because they have stopped being frightened of their own depth. Whatever emotion is moving through the situation — yours or someone else's — can be held now without breaking the container. Trust your judgment, especially about people. The King of Cups reads situations the way a stone reads water: by letting it move past without losing shape.
king-of-cups.reversed: Emotion is being swallowed instead of understood, or control is being mistaken for mastery. The reversed King suggests either a numbing that looks like calm, or a rigidity that cannot flex when flexibility would save you. Something that needs to be felt is being managed instead.
king-of-cups.love: Someone who has already survived their own heart and knows how to hold yours without crushing it.
king-of-cups.work: Judgment about people and situations that proves reliable. You can see the pattern because you have stopped needing the outcome to be a certain way.
king-of-cups.sajuLens: Water — 水 — is the King of Cups' native element: the capacity to receive, to flow, to reach equilibrium. But this card is water that has learned structure from 金 (metal). For a water Day Master, this reads as your natural skill finally finding its form — you have always felt deeply; now you know what to do with it. For a 火 (fire) Day Master, the card suggests learning to cool strategic thinking with emotional intelligence rather than burning through relationships on principle alone. A 木 (wood) Day Master sees it as reaching the growth phase where expansion becomes sustainable. 金 (metal) finds in it the validation that boundaries can hold without breaking. And 土 (earth) — already stable — gets permission to deepen without losing balance.

ace-of-swords.title: Ace of Swords
ace-of-swords.summary: The Ace of Swords cuts through confusion with a single stroke. Firm decision, clear thinking, the moment before action. What it means upright, reversed, and through a saju lens.
meaning: The Ace of Swords is metal at its sharpest: a Joseon hwando emerging from a clenched fist, point aimed straight up. This is not a weapon drawn in anger but a tool held in certainty. The card marks the instant when scattered thoughts crystallize into a single, undeniable truth — not after you have lived with it for months, but the moment it arrives and you suddenly cannot unsee it. Once you know, you know.

What distinguishes this card from mere thinking is the weight of commitment behind it. The sword has a crown and laurel branches wrapped around it because this kind of clarity does not come cheap. It costs you the comfort of ambiguity, the option to hedge your bets, the privilege of holding contradictory beliefs simultaneously. Metal cuts; it divides what was tangled into what is separate. The price of that clarity is choice.

symbols.label: The hwando pointing upward
symbols.text: A Joseon ceremonial sword emerging straight toward the sky. Vertical swords in tarot classically mean truth ascending, thought that has stopped circling and begun climbing. The hwando's specific form — the blade of Korean nobility — makes this a decision with weight behind it, not a casual opinion.

symbols.label: The clenched armored fist
symbols.text: The sword is held, not falling. This is not inspiration happening to you; it is conviction you are gripping. The armor confirms it: this clarity has been forged through some kind of pressure or test. The hand does not shake.

symbols.label: The crown and laurel branches
symbols.text: Victory markers twined around the blade itself. The card suggests that this particular truth, once claimed, carries authority with it — either because others will recognize it, or because you will need that recognition to hold the line.

symbols.label: Stormy mountain peaks below
symbols.text: The sword rises above weather and elevation. It points above the chaos. The storm is not resolved, but from the height this blade reaches, you can see the terrain clearly enough to move.

ace-of-swords.upright: Something is now undeniable. You have moved from analysis to knowing, from weighing options to having made a choice — perhaps without realizing exactly when it happened. The card asks you to commit to that clarity rather than slipping back into doubt. This is the moment to name what you now see, to draw the line you have been avoiding, to say the thing you can no longer keep private. Act on it before the feeling fades.
ace-of-swords.reversed: The sword is falling or the clarity is false. Either you are mistaking certainty for rigidity — holding a position too tightly because you need to believe you are right — or the truth you thought you had has already begun to unravel. Check whether your conviction is based on what you actually see or on what you need to believe.
ace-of-swords.love: A decision made; the haze lifts and you see clearly what you want or what you cannot accept.
ace-of-swords.work: A clear direction emerges, or a point needs to be made without softening. The time for negotiation or ambiguity is passing.
ace-of-swords.sajuLens: Swords are 金(metal), and the Ace carries metal's signature gesture: separation, precision, the moment when something unclear becomes defined. For a 金 Day Master — someone whose chart is already saturated with metal — this card often reads as confirmation of something they have already decided, a validation of the directness that comes naturally. For a 木(wood) Day Master, whose instinct runs toward expansion and softening the edges, the Ace can feel harsh or premature; it asks whether clarity sometimes needs to cut to be useful. For 火(fire), the card harmonizes — fire appreciates swift action. For 土(earth), which prefers stability through consensus, it may feel destabilizing. For 水(water), which values flow and perspective-shifting, the sword's fixed point can feel like rigidity, even when that rigidity is exactly what is needed.

two-of-swords.title: Two of Swords
two-of-swords.summary: Two of Swords shows a standstill: perfect balance held at cost. What it means upright, reversed, and through a saju lens.
meaning: The Two of Swords is a card of stalemate dressed as equilibrium. Two forces meet at exactly equal weight and neither moves. What looks like balance from outside reads from inside as exhaustion — the energy required to hold two opposing truths at the same time without letting either one fall. The blindfold matters. Not because the sitter cannot see clearly, but because looking clearly would mean choosing, and choosing would mean the other thing wins.

In 金(metal)'s language, this is a card about the edge that cuts both ways. Metal brings definition, but definition requires drawing a line. Before the line is drawn there is only potential; after it, there is loss. The Two of Swords is what lives in the moment just before that happens — the instant when both options are still alive because neither has been named the chosen one.

symbols.label: The blindfold
symbols.text: Not ornament. The figure cannot see the bay behind the rock boundary, cannot see which blade is which. The blind choice is the only choice that preserves the tie. Sight would force resolution.

symbols.label: Two swords crossed at the chest
symbols.text: Held in perfect balance against her own body. The weapons are not drawn against an enemy; they are held against the self. This is an internal conflict dressed as external stand-off.

symbols.label: The crescent moon and silver light
symbols.text: Neither full nor dark. The moon here is Metal's reflection without Metal's heat — cool, partial, refusing to illuminate the whole picture. Enough light to create shadow, not enough to eliminate it.

symbols.label: The rock boundary and frozen bay
symbols.text: The sea is contained but not crossed. The rocks form a wall that neither protects nor releases. Everything is held in suspension — movement is possible but not yet taken.

two-of-swords.upright: You are caught between two commitments of equal weight and neither will give. This is not a moment for forcing a decision; it is a moment for recognizing that the stalemate itself contains information. The card often points to a choice that looks like it has two options but actually has three: the two you can see, and the option of not choosing yet. Sit with the tension a little longer. Something will shift — someone always blinks first.
two-of-swords.reversed: The balance breaks. One blade falls and you are forced to act, or you abandon the swords entirely and walk away unarmed. Reversed, the Two often points to a decision finally made, but sometimes it points to someone who chose inaction and is now dealing with the consequences of that choice being made for them.
two-of-swords.love: Two people keeping their distance by keeping their weapons equally drawn.
two-of-swords.work: A project or partnership in perfect deadlock. Progress requires someone to lower their guard first.
two-of-swords.sajuLens: Metal 金 naturally reads this card as its own element in stasis — the precision and boundary-drawing that Metal excels at, frozen before it can land. For a 금(金) Day Master, Two of Swords often reads as a familiar state: the weight of holding multiple commitments in equilibrium, the control required to let nothing fall. This is how you already live. The question is whether the stalemate is serving you or costing you. For a 목(木) — wood Day Master, the card reads as a constraint: wood wants to grow and expand, and this is a card that says expand nowhere. For 화(火) — fire, it is frustration. Fire seeks expression and resolution; the blindfold and the standoff feel like suffocation. Water 수(水) reads it as a mirror — water also adapts to the container it is in. The card may be showing you a situation where you have succeeded too well at balancing opposing forces.

three-of-swords.title: Three of Swords
three-of-swords.summary: Three of Swords: heartbreak rendered in steel and rain. What the card means when it arrives upright, reversed, and read through the five elements.
meaning: Three ceremonial swords have pierced a single red silk heart. There are no figures here — no one to blame, no one to comfort, only the wound itself rendered in symbol. This is the card of sorrow arriving without narrative, the moment when pain has moved past story and become physical fact. The storm clouds and rain deepen the isolation: weather that no one controls, that changes nothing, that simply falls.

What makes this card bearable is that it does not pretend the swords will come out painlessly or that the heart will be unscathed. It acknowledges grief as a process rather than a failure. The three blades suggest that some wounds arrive in stages, or that the same hurt lands from multiple directions. The silk heart remains whole enough to hold the swords — it has not shattered. That distinction matters.

symbols.label: Three Joseon ceremonial swords
symbols.text: Metal piercing: sharp, unavoidable, formal. These are not crude weapons but ceremonial blades, suggesting that even deliberate harm carries a kind of order. Three suggests repetition, layering, or harm arriving from different angles simultaneously.

symbols.label: Red silk heart-shaped cushion
symbols.text: The heart is soft and precious but it is not fragile — it holds the swords without tearing. Red signals intensity, blood, the exposed centre. Silk speaks to something that was beautiful before the wound, and will require tending after.

symbols.label: Dark stormclouds and heavy rain
symbols.text: Weather that cannot be stopped or negotiated with. The storm frames grief as environmental fact rather than personal failure. Rain obscures, saturates, and washes — it does not heal but it does move things along.

three-of-swords.upright: Pain has arrived and it is real. This card does not offer false comfort or suggest the hurt will disappear if you think about it differently — it says: this has happened, you are wounded, and the wound will take time. The three swords imply that some griefs arrive in layers or from multiple sources at once. What matters now is not preventing the sorrow but moving through it without collapsing. The storm will not last forever, but it will not end on your schedule either.
three-of-swords.reversed: Either the pain is being avoided rather than felt, or it has already passed and you are still describing yourself as wounded. Reversed, the card points to sorrow becoming a habit, a identity rather than an event. Check whether you are still grieving or whether you have begun performing grief instead.
three-of-swords.love: A breaking point, or a moment when the relationship absorbs a hurt that changes its shape permanently.
three-of-swords.work: A setback that cuts deep, or a decision that requires accepting loss before moving forward.
three-of-swords.sajuLens: 火 — fire charts often read this card as activation rather than mere pain: the swords as cautery, burning away what needs to go. 木 — wood people experience it as blockage, growth halted mid-season. 土 — earth finds the storm destabilizing and the fixed heart-shape a small comfort. 金 — metal recognizes the swords as their own element turned inward; the card asks what precision and structure are serving. 水 — water charts sometimes find this card less jarring — flowing through sorrow is closer to their native work. If your Day Master is 金 — metal, the swords may feel like control or discipline; if it is 火 — fire, they may read as necessary burning.

four-of-swords.title: Four of Swords
four-of-swords.summary: Rest earned after conflict. The Four of Swords is metal 金 in stillness — a pause that stabilizes rather than heals, and a quiet that asks what you do with it.
meaning: The Four of Swords shows a general in full armor lying motionless on stone, hands clasped as if in prayer or simply held still. Three swords hang on the wall above him; one lies beneath the slab. The arrangement is not a victory—it reads as a cessation, a moment when the body stops moving and the mind is permitted to follow. This is metal 金 at rest: the hardness of armor, the weight of discipline, the clarity that comes only when you stop generating motion.

What the card describes is not peace but interruption. The general has not retired; he has paused. The swords remain—three waiting, one beneath—and the stillness is temporary by design. Recovery here is functional: you are refilling a reserve that was not infinite, learning what you can think when you are not defending. The colored light from the lotus window suggests that even rest can contain ritual, that lying still is not the same as being empty.

symbols.label: The general in full armor
symbols.text: He wears the weight he earned. The card does not suggest removing the armor or leaving it behind—just that the body can be still inside it. This is rest for someone whose vigilance runs bone-deep, not relaxation but deliberate cessation.

symbols.label: Three swords on the wall, one beneath
symbols.text: The fourth sword is directly under his body, closest and lowest. The arrangement suggests that not all conflict is over—only this particular conflict, this particular moment of intensity. The others wait in view, a reminder rather than a threat.

symbols.label: Stone slab and temple chamber
symbols.text: The setting is formal, consecrated, held apart from ordinary time. This is not a nap between tasks but a deliberate removal from circulation, a space designed for the transition between states.

symbols.label: Stained glass lotus light, pale stone, amber warmth
symbols.text: Color and shadow are layered into monochrome grey. The light is present but filtered, gentle without being soft. Recovery here happens inside a frame, with attention and intention.

four-of-swords.upright: You have earned the right to stop. The Four of Swords does not ask you to forgive what happened or to forget—only to lay it down long enough to remember what you sound like when you are not reacting to it. Stay in the stillness until your mind quiets, not until your circumstances change. This is not a retreat; it is a refueling that requires you to be completely still in order to work.
four-of-swords.reversed: The pause is not being honored. Either you are pushing yourself back into motion before the reserve has filled, or the stillness itself has begun to feel like a trap. Check whether rest has become avoidance, and whether the armor is being worn as a reason not to move rather than as something you will wear again when you leave.
four-of-swords.love: Distance or silence right now—not rejection, but both of you catching breath.
four-of-swords.work: Take the break you have earned before the next phase. Productivity will move faster if you stop accelerating first.
four-of-swords.sajuLens: The Four of Swords is 金(metal) in absolute stillness, and it reads entirely differently depending on whether your Day Master is metal or not. If your 일간 is 庚(metal) or 辛(metal), this card often arrives as an affirmation—you already understand the rhythm of tension and deliberate pause, and this is simply marking where you are in the cycle. If your Day Master is 木(wood)—the impulse to grow and expand—the Four of Swords can feel like imprisonment, and the reading shifts: rest is being imposed, not chosen. For 火(fire) Day Masters, it reads as necessary dampening; for 水(water), as the still place you need; for 土(earth), as the holding pattern that precedes a new foundation. Your element determines whether stillness reads as natural rhythm or as temporary frustration.

five-of-swords.title: Five of Swords
five-of-swords.summary: The Five of Swords is a hollow victory — the cost of winning by any means. What it means upright, reversed, and through a saju lens.
meaning: This is the card of the pyrrhic outcome. The warrior has taken what he came for, and the field is littered with the proof: three swords gathered, opponents in retreat. But the grey sea and torn sky suggest that the ground beneath the victory has already begun to shift. What was won this way does not hold. The smirk on his face is not triumph — it is the expression of someone who has just realized that the prize tastes like nothing at all.

The Five of Swords describes the moment when you understand that achieving an aim by any means available has left you with the aim but not with what you actually wanted. It is not about failure. It is about success that costs more than it yields. The card asks: what did you keep, and what did you lose in order to keep it? The two figures walking away are not your enemies — they are what you left behind.

symbols.label: The warrior's smirk
symbols.text: Not satisfaction. The expression is already turning inward, toward the small cold knowledge that this victory is not what he thought it would be. The cost has become visible too late.

symbols.label: Three swords gathered from the ground
symbols.text: He has what he came for. But notice that they are all gathered in one grip — unstable, difficult to hold, impossible to use. This is what winning-at-all-costs looks like in practice.

symbols.label: Two figures walking away in the distance
symbols.text: They are not running in panic. The dejectedness is the card's true subject — these are the relationships, the principles, or the trust you surrendered in order to keep the swords.

symbols.label: The choppy grey sea and storm-torn sky
symbols.text: No solid ground. The landscape confirms what the expression already suggests: whatever you won here will not stay won. The instability is built in.

five-of-swords.upright: You have achieved something by methods you would not defend if asked to explain them. The victory is real but the foundation underneath it is already eroding. Pause before celebrating. The question now is not whether you won, but whether keeping this particular prize is worth what has been hollowed out in the winning. Sometimes the answer is yes — but not until you have actually counted the cost.
five-of-swords.reversed: The means have caught up with you before the end could justify them. Reversed, the Five of Swords often points to a scheme collapsing or a victory being taken back because the methods are now known. The other choice is to stop before you finish — to set the swords down and walk away, which is sometimes the only thing that still looks like winning.
five-of-swords.love: Someone won an argument and lost the relationship.
five-of-swords.work: You are getting what you asked for by burning capital you did not know you were spending.
five-of-swords.sajuLens: 金(metal) — the element of this card — is sharp, final, and leaves no ambiguity about boundaries. For a metal Day Master (庚, 辛), the Five of Swords often reads as a necessary correction: you have cut away what needed cutting, and yes, it looks harsh. The card reassures more than it warns. But for 火(fire) Day Masters (丙, 丁), who need reciprocity and witness, this card arrives as genuine cautionary weight — you are winning in a way that isolates. For 木(wood) Day Masters, the card points to expansion that has turned rigid and hostile. The remedy is different for each: metal restores through acceptance, fire through reconnection, wood through flexibility. 土(earth) reads it as a permanent rupture; 水(water) as an illusion of control about to shatter.

six-of-swords.title: Six of Swords
six-of-swords.summary: The Six of Swords moves from turbulent waters toward calm — a Joseon ferryman's passage from trouble to safety. What it means upright, reversed, and through a saju lens.
meaning: The Six of Swords is motion with weight. A ferryman poles a wooden boat across a river, a woman and child huddled in the bow, six swords planted upright in the prow like a fence or a ward. The waters behind are rough and choppy; ahead they smooth into grey-blue calm. This is not escape as flight — there is no panic here, only steady work. The passage takes time. Someone is doing the labour of moving you from one state to another.

The card describes a turning situation where the direction is already established but the arrival is not immediate. You are leaving trouble behind, yes, but you cannot skip the crossing. The mist suggests you cannot see far ahead either. What matters is that the current is running toward shelter, and that someone knows how to read the water well enough to pole through it. This is the card of the situation that is already improving, even though improvement still has distance to cover.

symbols.label: The ferryman poling steadily
symbols.text: He is not rowing frantically or fighting the current. His work is methodical and competent — the kind of labour that moves you because it knows the river. The passage itself is the point. Without the ferryman's skill, the destination would not matter.

symbols.label: Six upright swords in the prow
symbols.text: Metal swords planted like sentinels, standing between the passengers and the rough water. They are not drawn or raised — they are rooted, forming a barrier or a boundary. Protection through structure and firmness, not through aggression.

symbols.label: Woman and child huddled in the bow
symbols.text: They are the cargo, the reason for the crossing. They are not steering or working. Their job is to stay put and trust the ferryman's knowledge. Vulnerability is allowed here because passage is being managed by someone steady.

symbols.label: Rough water becoming calm
symbols.text: The transition from choppy to smooth marks the arc of the card — not a sudden shift but a gradient, a slow settling. The muted grey-blue and pale morning light suggest emergence from something darker into something gentler, though not yet bright.

six-of-swords.upright: You are moving away from turbulence, but the crossing itself still requires patience and steady work. This is not the card of escape — it is the card of managed passage. Trust the ferryman, whoever or whatever that is: the process, the person helping, the plan that is already in motion. Stay low and let the current carry you. The swords are there; the direction is set. What you cannot do yet is see the far shore clearly, and that is fine.
six-of-swords.reversed: The crossing is stalling or the direction is uncertain. Either the ferryman has lost his way in the mist, or the passengers are fighting the boat's motion, or the swords that were meant to protect are now keeping something trapped. The water may be growing rough again. Check whether you are actually moving or whether you have stopped midstream.
six-of-swords.love: A relationship in transition — moving from one state toward another, with both people understanding they are in the crossing, not yet at the destination.
six-of-swords.work: A project or role in managed transition. You are being moved toward a better position by something external; your job is to keep steady during the passage.
six-of-swords.sajuLens: The Six of Swords is 金 (metal) — swords are metal, the structure is metal, the boundary holds. Metal is about definition, containment, moving from disorder into form. For a metal Day Master — 庚(geng) or 辛(sin) — this card reads as natural: you understand the logic of protective barriers and steady method. For 木 (wood) Day Masters, the six upright swords can feel restrictive, like being caged in order to be saved; the crossing works, but it costs you motion and flexibility. For 火 (fire), the muted grey-blue light and the passive waiting read as dimming; for 水 (water), the ferryman's competence and the clear direction feel like shelter. For 土 (earth), the steady passage and the defined endpoint offer grounding.

seven-of-swords.title: Seven of Swords
seven-of-swords.summary: The Seven of Swords is a card of calculated theft — a move made in the half-light, carrying what you can while leaving traces behind. What it means upright, reversed, and through a saju lens.
meaning: This is the card of the theft that works, at least for now. The trickster in this image is already halfway gone, five swords bundled under his arm, two left in the grass as decoys or simply abandoned because greed would slow him down. He knows exactly how many he can carry and he is moving. The 金 — metal element of Swords is at its sharpest here: the ability to cut through, to separate what is yours from what is not, to know the difference between strategy and stupidity by the width of a blade.

But notice he glances back. That glance contains the card's real message. A successful theft leaves someone behind discovering the loss. The Seven of Swords is not about getting away clean — it is about the moment before you find out whether you actually got away at all. Upright, it reads as a move made with eyes open to the cost. You are taking something that was not given, and you are aware of that fact. The question is whether the taking was necessary.

symbols.label: Five swords bundled under one arm
symbols.text: He takes what he can carry and no more. This is not panic or indiscriminate grabbing — it is a clear decision about capacity. The grip itself requires calculation: too loose and they scatter, too tight and he cannot move. The number five marks a threshold between manageable theft and recklessness.

symbols.label: Two swords left behind in the grass
symbols.text: Either abandoned mid-grab or left as a deliberate misdirection, they matter more than the ones he took. They prove he was here. They also prove he did not take everything, which sometimes makes a theft believable in a way that total clearing does not.

symbols.label: The glance back over his shoulder
symbols.text: He knows he might be seen. The sly grin suggests he is betting on the dark and the dawn confusion to buy time, but he is not stupid enough to believe he is invisible. This is the moment before consequences catch up, held in a glance that knows what it has done.

symbols.label: Orange sunrise silhouetting the camp tents
symbols.text: Dawn exposes. The light is rising and the encampment is still asleep, but that window is closing by the second. The orange and grey colour scheme marks a boundary between night's cover and day's accountability. He is leaving exactly when he should.

seven-of-swords.upright: Something has been taken or leaked or moved without permission, and it worked well enough to feel justified. The card does not judge the theft — it only marks it clearly as a theft, made by someone who understood the risk and moved anyway. If this is your move, you are betting on speed and on the fact that by the time the loss is noticed, the ground will have shifted enough that retrieval will seem unimportant. That calculation might be correct. But keep moving — hesitation is what gets thieves caught.
seven-of-swords.reversed: The theft did not work, or it is about to not work. Reversed, the trickster is moving too slowly, carrying too much, or has already been seen. Someone is awake in those tents. What seemed like a clean move has left too many traces, and the glance back has become a moment of recognition. The recklessness that felt bold now feels simply reckless.
seven-of-swords.love: Someone is keeping something back, or has already decided to take what was not offered.
seven-of-swords.work: A shortcut that saves time now and costs it later. Quick but unclean.
seven-of-swords.sajuLens: The Seven of Swords is 金 — metal: the cutting, separating force that divides mine from yours and moves with decisive speed. For a metal 일간 (Day Master) — 庚(geng) or 辛(xin) — this card often reads as strategy, even permission, because separation and risk-taking are already native to how you operate. For a wood 일간 (木), it lands harder: 木 expands, connects, builds relationship; a sword theft cuts those threads. For water 일간 (水), the card points to a clever move that solves nothing, because water flows and returns; stolen goods have a way of finding their way back to the surface. Earth 일간 (土) reads it as destabilization: the ground beneath trust has been cut away and will not resettle quickly.

eight-of-swords.title: Eight of Swords
eight-of-swords.summary: Eight of Swords shows a mind locked in by its own thinking. The bonds are loose enough to break, but she cannot see that. What it means upright, reversed, and through a saju lens.
meaning: The Eight of Swords is not about external imprisonment. The Joseon noblewoman stands blindfolded and loosely bound with red rope, circled by eight upright swords — but the restraints are slack enough to slip free if she moved. The card's whole point is that the cage is mostly made of her own refusal to try. Behind her, a fortress stands in storm. She has mistaken caution for captivity.

What matters here is the blindfold. She cannot see the space around her, cannot see that the swords form a circle rather than a wall, cannot see that escape is a matter of three steps in any direction. The card describes the moment when thought becomes a locked room — when you have rehearsed a single story about what is possible so many times that you no longer check whether it is still true.

symbols.label: The blindfold
symbols.text: She cannot see the gaps between the swords. The Eight of Swords is not about walls but about not looking — the mind refusing information that would change the calculation. This is self-imposed darkness, which makes it both more frustrating and more reversible than actual darkness.

symbols.label: The loose red rope
symbols.text: The binding is ornamental rather than functional. Red, in Korean tradition, often signals intention or will rather than accident. These are the restraints she has woven for herself, the rules she has internalized so completely that she no longer notices they are rules.

symbols.label: The eight upright swords in a circle
symbols.text: They form an enclosure, but not a prison — there are gaps. The swords are 金 — metal energy made visible. They represent boundaries, definitions, the edges that create shape. Here they create an illusion of enclosure rather than an actual one.

symbols.label: The storm and the fortress
symbols.text: Behind her stands a real threat — the fort suggests actual danger exists somewhere. But she is not in the fortress; she is outside it, in her own mind. The card separates the danger she fears from the one she has actually created.

eight-of-swords.upright: You are more confined by what you believe than by what is actually true. The Eight of Swords arrives when a mind has circled the same calculation so many times that it stops checking for exits. Take the blindfold off — not metaphorically, but as a first action. Look at the actual situation rather than the story you have been telling about it. The ropes are looser than you think.
eight-of-swords.reversed: Either the blindfold is coming off or you are pushing harder against bonds that will not break. Reversed, the card can read as dawning awareness — the moment you see that escape was possible all along. But it can also read as desperation, thrashing against a constraint you have misdiagnosed. Check whether you are actually trapped or whether you have simply decided to stay.
eight-of-swords.love: Fear of commitment disguised as lack of choice. The other person cannot free you; only you can remove the blindfold.
eight-of-swords.work: You have stopped trying because you have already decided it will not work. The constraint is real until you test it.
eight-of-swords.sajuLens: The Eight of Swords is 金 — metal: structure, definition, the mind making distinctions and building walls. For a 金 Day Master, this card often reads as self-recognition — you see how your own need for order has created a perimeter. For 木 — wood Day Masters, who move forward by instinct and tend not to second-guess themselves, the Eight of Swords appears as a warning about someone else's thinking, or as a moment when your usual momentum has been interrupted by overthinking. For 火 — fire, the card suggests passion has been extinguished by analysis. For 土 — earth, it points to worry habits that have hardened into walls. For 水 — water, the blindfold prevents you from feeling your way forward, which is usually water's strongest tool.

nine-of-swords.title: Nine of Swords
nine-of-swords.summary: Anxiety carved into the night. Nine of Swords is the card of spiralling dread, where fear has already won the argument with reason. What it means upright, reversed, and through a saju lens.
meaning: Nine of Swords is a card about the hour when sleep has failed and your own mind has become the enemy. The figure sits rigid in darkness, clutching their head as if it might otherwise shatter. Nine 金(metal) swords hang on the wall like a sentence already passed — not a threat approaching, but judgment already rendered and nailed in place. This is anxiety that has stopped being useful and become architectural. The carved panels on the bed frame show defeat. The swords are cold. Nothing here is metaphorical.

What distinguishes this card from its cousins is the specific texture of the torment: it is not external danger but internal recursion. The swords are not falling. They are waiting. The figure has created a prison from their own worst-case thinking and now lives inside it, playing the catastrophe again and again until it feels like memory instead of invention. The card describes the moment when you are no longer fighting the fear — you are only fighting sleep, and losing.

symbols.label: The nine swords on the wall
symbols.text: Sharp, identical, arranged in a row like an inventory of all the ways this could go wrong. They are not attacking — they are on display. The arrangement is methodical, almost bureaucratic. This is what happens when anxiety becomes systematic.

symbols.label: The figure bolt upright
symbols.text: Not tossing in sleep but fully awake and wound tight enough to snap. The posture is rigid, the grip on their own head suggesting they are holding something in that might otherwise escape. Tension this complete is also a form of control.

symbols.label: The carved panels showing defeat
symbols.text: The bed itself carries a record of loss. This is not the first time this person has slept here, and memory is built into the furniture. The past is part of the architecture.

symbols.label: Deep indigo darkness and cold grey
symbols.text: Not the black of true night but the specific darkness of 3 a.m., when time feels broken. The grey of the swords reads as metal in its purest form: hard, reflective, without warmth or give.

nine-of-swords.upright: This card arrives when the thinking has curdled and repetition has replaced reason. You are running the same loop through your head because stopping feels like surrender. The swords on the wall are not going to move — only you can. That usually means naming the actual fear instead of the ten versions of it you have assembled, or it means accepting that you cannot solve this at 3 a.m. and giving yourself permission to wait until morning. The card often appears when someone has been treating anxiety like a problem to be thought through rather than a state to be moved through.
nine-of-swords.reversed: The grip loosens. Reversed, the Nine of Swords suggests the moment when you stop fighting the fear and it loses its grip on you — not because the worry has resolved, but because you have stopped treating your own thinking as prophecy. The crisis passes. The swords remain on the wall, but you have stopped staring at them. This card reversed often marks the other side of the spiral, the moment when sleep returns and the night releases you.
nine-of-swords.love: Anxiety about attachment that has calcified into certainty — the story you tell yourself about why this will fail is now more real to you than the person across from you.
nine-of-swords.work: Fretting has become the default, and the mental loops around the task have replaced the work itself. Productivity has stalled because you are too busy rehearsing all the ways it could go wrong.
nine-of-swords.sajuLens: Nine of Swords is 金(metal) in extremis: sharp, precise, endlessly refined. 金(Metal) rules structure, boundaries, and the cutting-away of excess — but in its shadow form it becomes rigidity, perfectionism, the blade turned inward. If your 일간 (Day Master) is 金(metal), this card often reads as a mirror: your precision can calcify into obsession, your standards into cruelty directed at yourself. If your chart leans 木(wood) — which seeks expansion and trusts the unfinished — this card feels foreign and troubling: something in you recognizes it as a mode you can fall into but do not naturally inhabit. For 火(fire) charts, the anxiety reads as particularly agonizing because fire wants to move and act, and the rigidity here is paralyzing.

ten-of-swords.title: Ten of Swords
ten-of-swords.summary: The final blow has landed. Ten of Swords is the card of rock bottom, acceptance, and the strange peace that comes when there is nothing left to defend.
meaning: The Ten of Swords looks like a ending, and it is — but not the kind that breaks you. This is what happens after the breaking is already done. The figure lies face-down in white hanbok with ten swords planted precisely in their back, and their raised hand is not a gesture of resistance but of surrender. The night has passed. The horizon holds a golden sunrise. Rock bottom, it turns out, is also a place from which you can finally rest.

In saju terms, this is 金(metal) at its limit: the principle of containment, of form, of edges pressed to their absolute boundary. When you reach it, something unexpected happens. The weight of all those swords becomes weightlessness. The struggle stops because there is nowhere left to fall. What the card marks is not the harm itself but the threshold you cross when you stop fighting it.

symbols.label: The ten swords in a line
symbols.text: Precise. Deliberate. Not chaotic but arranged like a meditation. The number ten completes a cycle — there is nothing left to add, nothing left to do but accept what is already whole.

symbols.label: White hanbok and dawn gold
symbols.text: The figure wears ritual white, the Korean colour of mourning and of renewal. The golden sunrise behind them is not cruel contrast but genuine promise — the darkest night has actually passed, and proof is already arriving on the horizon.

symbols.label: The raised hand in peace
symbols.text: Not fallen in defeat but held in a gesture of release. This hand is not fighting anymore. It is the pose of someone who has chosen to lay down the weight they have carried.

symbols.label: Calm sea and stillness
symbols.text: There is no storm, no struggle in the landscape. Everything is quiet. Rock bottom is not frantic — it is the last place where urgency finally dies.

ten-of-swords.upright: You have reached the end of something and you know it. There is a strange relief in this card, because fighting is over — not because you won, but because surrender has its own completeness. What comes next will not look like continuation. It will look like starting over. For now, the only instruction is to lay it down and let yourself be still.
