ten-of-swords.reversed: The swords are still there but you are not finished absorbing the blow. Reversed, this card suggests you are still braced for impact, still defending yourself against something that has already happened. The peace the card offers is available, but you have not yet stepped into it.
ten-of-swords.love: Relationship has run its course and there is no point in reopening old cuts.
ten-of-swords.work: A project or role has reached its natural end, even if you are not ready to name it yet.
ten-of-swords.sajuLens: Ten of Swords is 金(metal) completed — the principle of structure, boundaries, and precision taken to the point where it must transform or collapse. Someone with 金 as their Day Master may read this card as necessary closure, a clean cut that allows something new to form. But for a 木(wood) Day Master, whose nature is expansion and forward momentum, this card lands harder — it requires sitting still in a way that feels like suffocation. For 水(water) Day Master — fluid, adaptive — the acceptance comes more naturally, though the message may feel like resignation. 火(fire) will resist the passivity. 土(earth) will understand it as grounding, as finally having solid ground beneath.

page-of-swords.title: Page of Swords
page-of-swords.summary: The Page of Swords is watchfulness before action — a young soldier scanning for what comes next. What it means upright, reversed, and through a saju lens.
meaning: The Page of Swords is the card of preparation that has not yet become paranoia. He stands on high ground with his sword raised, feet ready to spring, eyes fixed on the horizon. He is not attacking; he is listening. Metal — 金 — is the element of sharpness, of definition, of knowing exactly where one thing ends and another begins. This page has that quality turned outward: he sees the shape of what is coming before it arrives.

What distinguishes him from anxiety is that his alertness is still calm. His uniform is practice white, not battle-stained. The storms and birds around him are facts he has already noticed and sorted. He is the card of someone who has trained enough to be dangerous without needing to prove it yet — the watcher who does not need to move because he has already decided what he will do when the moment comes.

symbols.label: Sword raised in both hands
symbols.text: The blade is high but not overhead — a ready position, not an attack. Both hands grip it, suggesting control and intention rather than improvisation. He is holding something he knows how to use.

symbols.label: Sharp keen eyes on the horizon
symbols.text: His gaze is the real weapon here. He scans the landscape for information, for the small shifts that tell you what is about to happen. This is intelligence gathering, not confrontation.

symbols.label: Feet nimble and ready to spring
symbols.text: His body is coiled but not tense — the difference between readiness and fear. He can move in any direction because he has not already committed his weight to one outcome.

symbols.label: White and grey practice uniform, stormy sky
symbols.text: The uniform says training, not war. The storms and racing clouds are the environment he moves through, not emotions he carries. He remains separate from the chaos around him.

page-of-swords.upright: You are gathering information before you move. The card favours the watcher, the one who asks questions before announcing answers, the person who trains in private so they will be dangerous in public. Do not mistake this for indecision — you know what you are looking for; you are simply patient enough to wait until you find it. Information is your weapon right now. Use it.
page-of-swords.reversed: The alertness has crossed over into suspicion or the preparation into paralysis. You are watching so carefully that you have forgotten to decide what happens when you see something. Either trust your training and move, or admit that you are afraid and sit with that instead of performing readiness.
page-of-swords.love: Too much watching, not enough vulnerability. You cannot read your way into intimacy.
page-of-swords.work: Intelligence work, research, or preparation. Someone else will execute; you are building the foundation they will stand on.
page-of-swords.sajuLens: The Page carries 金 — metal: the element of clarity, edges, discrimination. Metal Day Masters (庚 — geng, 辛 — xin) often read this page as simply describing how they naturally operate — they gather data, they notice patterns, they trust a sharp eye more than a comfortable feeling. For 木 — wood Day Masters (甲 — jia, 乙 — yi), this card can read as a necessary skill to develop, because wood's instinct is to expand and trust; the Page asks: what if you gathered a little more information first? For 火 — fire (丙 — bing, 丁 — ding), the page's calm can feel like a cage; for 水 — water (壬 — ren, 癸 — gui), it reads as natural kinship. For 土 — earth (戊 — wu, 己 — ji), it suggests useful but uncomfortable sharpness.

knight-of-swords.title: Knight of Swords
knight-of-swords.summary: The Knight of Swords charges through storm and doubt with unsheathed blade and absolute conviction. What it means upright, reversed, and through a saju lens.
meaning: This is the card of someone who has decided and is now simply moving. The Knight of Swords does not deliberate in the saddle — the deliberation happened before he mounted. Now there is only the gallop, the raised blade, the momentum that makes second-guessing impossible. He is a Joseon cavalry soldier in full armor, riding a black horse into a storm, and he will not turn back because turning back would require stopping, and stopping is not what he was built for.

What matters here is not whether the storm will break him. What matters is that he has chosen a direction so clearly that the direction itself becomes real. The wind tears at his horsehair plume, birds scatter around him, lightning splits the sky — and none of it changes his course by a degree. This is 金(metal) at its most refined: the blade that has been sharpened to a single point of purpose, the clarity that cuts through everything else.

symbols.label: The raised sword
symbols.text: High above his head, already committed. This is not a weapon held in readiness — it is already in motion. The arc of the swing is set before the enemy appears.

symbols.label: The black horse at full gallop
symbols.text: Sheer forward momentum. Every muscle is extended; there is no reserve left in hand. The horse and rider are already past the point where stopping is possible.

symbols.label: The stormy grey and steel blue
symbols.text: The world is chaos — violent wind, shattered sky, lightning in silver flashes. None of it touches his course. The colors are metal colors: hard, cold, unforgiving.

symbols.label: The wind-torn horsehair plume
symbols.text: His armor marks him as someone who has trained for this exact moment. The wind tears at it, the storm tests it, but the plume still stands. Training does not prevent the storm; it lets you ride through it anyway.

knight-of-swords.upright: Commit and move. You have done the thinking already — now the card is telling you to act on the conviction you have assembled, even though the conditions will never be perfect and the doubt will never fully clear. The Knight of Swords succeeds not because he knows he will win, but because he knows his own direction so clearly that hesitation becomes impossible. Cut away everything that is not the line you have chosen. Momentum is its own argument.
knight-of-swords.reversed: The charge is happening without the clarity that justifies it. You are riding hard toward something you have not fully decided on, or worse, riding hard away from something you are afraid of. The storm ahead looks like an obstacle when it might be a signal to check your compass. Reversed, this card suggests that speed is covering up doubt rather than replacing it.
knight-of-swords.love: A bold move made with full certainty. This person is not testing the water — they have already committed to the leap.
knight-of-swords.work: A decisive action taken rapidly, before committee and consensus have time to form. The moment belongs to the person who acts first and briefs afterward.
knight-of-swords.sajuLens: The Knight of Swords is 金(metal) — the element of sharpness, of edges, of a single point driven forward. For a 金 Day Master, this card usually reads as confirmation; you already work in straight lines and you already move fast. The card is simply telling you that speed is correct here. For a 木(wood) Day Master, who thinks in branches and spreads, the Knight arrives as pressure to narrow your focus: the sword cuts, wood expands, and this card is saying that expansion will lose you this particular battle. For 火(fire) Day Masters, the charge appeals to your intensity but warns that intensity without clear direction becomes scattered. For 水(water) and 土(earth) Day Masters — who naturally prefer flow and stability — the Knight reads as an invitation to move faster than feels safe, to trust the armor rather than the hesitation.

queen-of-swords.title: Queen of Swords
queen-of-swords.summary: The Queen of Swords cuts through sentiment to see what is actually there. Rational judgment, intellectual clarity, and the cost of seeing too well.
meaning: The Queen of Swords is the mind at its sharpest and coldest. She sits motionless on her throne, one hand raised in formal greeting—the gesture of someone who will engage on her own terms, not yours. She holds her sword upright, not as a weapon drawn in anger but as an instrument kept ready. What matters is not her severity but her precision: she sees the situation as it actually is, not as she wishes it to be. This is the card of clarity purchased at the price of detachment.

She is fiercely independent because she has learned not to depend on anyone else's version of the truth. The butterfly carved into her throne is ornament, not distraction—beauty that does not soften her judgment. The bird flying free behind her suggests a choice already made: clarity over comfort, self-possession over belonging. When she appears, something false is about to be named, or a decision is about to be made by someone who will not flinch from its consequences.

symbols.label: The upright sword
symbols.text: Held steady, not raised to strike. This is clarity as a tool, not aggression. The sword stays vertical: precise, uncompromising, ready. It cuts through what is unnecessary to see what remains.

symbols.label: The stone throne carved with a butterfly
symbols.text: Solid and permanent, yet decorated with something brief and fragile. She understands beauty and impermanence; they simply do not move her judgment. The throne is carved, deliberate—nothing accidental about her position.

symbols.label: The raised hand in formal greeting
symbols.text: A gesture of acknowledgment made at arm's length. She will engage, but on her conditions. This is how boundaries look when they are held by someone who will not negotiate them.

symbols.label: The grey-blue daeryebok and windswept sky
symbols.text: Austere colours, cold light. No warmth in the palette. The wind moves; she does not. The penetrating expression reads what the moment actually requires, not what sentiment prefers.

queen-of-swords.upright: A situation demands to be seen clearly, and you are the person willing to do it. The Queen of Swords cuts through the story everyone has agreed on to name what is actually happening. Her presence in a reading means the time for polite fictions has ended. Trust your perception, even when—especially when—it isolates you from the consensus. This is the card of the person who speaks the thing no one else will.
queen-of-swords.reversed: The clarity has turned into a weapon, or the isolation has become its own kind of hiding. Reversed, the Queen's sharpness can curdle into cruelty, or her independence can harden into loneliness. Check whether you are seeing truly or merely enjoying the feeling of being right. Some truths cut so cleanly because they have left the target untouched.
queen-of-swords.love: Someone choosing clarity over reassurance—either yourself or the person across from you.
queen-of-swords.work: You are needed for your judgment, not your agreement. Deliver the assessment everyone knows is coming and will resent you for giving.
queen-of-swords.sajuLens: The Queen of Swords is pure 金 (metal): the energy of definition, boundary, the blade that separates one thing from another. Metal rules autumn, endings, what must be cut away to see the structure underneath. For a metal Day Master—庚(geng) or 辛(xin) stems—this card often reads as a return home, a validation of how you already work: rational, unflinching, self-contained. Fire 日 (day) masters find her difficult; 火 (fire) wants connection and meaning, while she offers only truth. Wood 日 masters chafe against her limits. Earth 日 masters respect her but wish she would soften. Water 日 masters understand her isolation but live differently. The card's real question: are you being clear, or merely afraid?

king-of-swords.title: King of Swords
king-of-swords.summary: The King of Swords holds authority through clarity and precision. What it means upright, reversed, and through a saju lens.
meaning: The King of Swords is judgment made visible — not the messy argument before judgment, but the moment after, when one voice has been heard and the decision stands. He sits high enough that no one can mistake him for an equal. The sword before him is not drawn in anger; it is held upright as a tool of measure, the thing that divides what is true from what merely sounds true. His eyes are sharp enough to see the difference.

This is the card of someone who has learned that power flows toward clarity. He does not need to shout or threaten; his analysis is already decisive. In the KSaju deck he wears the deep blue of Joseon military authority, cranes and crescents carved into stone beneath him — signs of constancy and the passing night. Behind him the storm is clearing. He has already won the argument; what remains is only the administration of what he knows.

symbols.label: The upright sword
symbols.text: Held vertically before him, not raised in battle but displayed as the emblem of his authority. The sword is the weapon of the mind — it cuts through confusion and poor reasoning. That it stands still shows this is not about conflict but about judgment already rendered.

symbols.label: Deep blue armor with crane motifs
symbols.text: The blue is 金 — metal in its coldest form, the colour of steel and clarity. Cranes are birds of longevity and wisdom in East Asian tradition. The armor protects nothing soft; this is a man whose power lies entirely in his thinking.

symbols.label: The stone throne carved with butterflies and moon
symbols.text: Permanence underneath transience. The butterflies and crescent suggest that his authority, though solid, is also aware of time and impermanence. He holds power but does not mistake it for immortality.

symbols.label: Sharp clear intelligent eyes and clearing sky
symbols.text: The weather has changed because his mind is clear. The storm behind him is not threatening him but retreating. His gaze cuts through what confused others — this is what it looks like when understanding wins.

king-of-swords.upright: A decision that cannot be argued with. Someone (possibly you) has thought past the obvious and reached the thing that is actually true. This is not cruelty; it is the mercy of knowing which way is which. Act from this clarity and expect others to follow, because people trust precision more than they trust kindness. The King of Swords reads as permission to be right out loud.
king-of-swords.reversed: The clarity has turned into rigidity or, worse, into the appearance of clarity where none exists. A reversed King of Swords is often someone using sharp language to win arguments they are actually losing, or enforcing a decision that looks decisive but was not actually thought through. Check whether you are being precise or just loud.
king-of-swords.love: Someone who thinks first and feels second — attractive to people who value understanding, difficult for people who need to feel valued first.
king-of-swords.work: Strategic analysis, judgment calls, roles where being right matters more than being liked. The person who can see what everyone else is missing.
king-of-swords.sajuLens: 金 — metal is the King of Swords' home element: boundary-making, discrimination, the knife that separates one thing from another. For a metal Day Master (庚, 辛), this card often reads as natural authority — you are describing how metal already operates, cutting clean through muddle. For 木 — wood Day Masters (甲, 乙), the King of Swords arrives as a necessary tension: wood expands, metal contracts, and their difference is where real decisions live. Wood finds the King initially cold, but learns that his clarity is useful. 火 — fire and 水 — water Day Masters often experience this card as external constraint — a power that is real but not native to how they think.

ace-of-pentacles.title: Ace of Pentacles
ace-of-pentacles.summary: The Ace of Pentacles is the first card of the suit — a single gleaming coin held aloft, the tangible reward that arrives when effort has finally assembled into something real.
meaning: The Ace of Pentacles is not luck. It is the moment when work converts into matter. A hand emerges from golden cloud to offer you a brass 엽전, a Korean coin with a square hole at its center — the kind that stacked into actual money, into actual power. Behind it lies a path through a garden of chrysanthemums and peonies leading to distant mountains. The card describes not the wish but the first solid thing you can hold that proves the wish was never only wishful.

Earth element cards speak in the language of consequences. This one says: what you built is real now. You can trade it, plant it, let it grow into more. The path through the garden is open, which means the reward is not an ending but a threshold. The distant mountains suggest there is still distance to travel, but you will not travel it empty-handed.

symbols.label: The gleaming brass coin
symbols.text: The 엽전 holds weight and history. Its square hole marks it as currency, as something that moves between hands and accumulates value. Brass catches light — what you have earned is visible, not theoretical.

symbols.label: The hand emerging from golden cloud
symbols.text: Reward does not fall from nowhere. The cloud suggests source, favour, the invisible infrastructure of effort finally paying out. The hand is the bridge between effort and receipt.

symbols.label: Garden archway of chrysanthemums and peonies
symbols.text: Both flowers carry meaning in Korean tradition: chrysanthemums mark steadiness and longevity, peonies mark prosperity and good fortune. The archway frames the reward as a passage, not a dead end.

symbols.label: Distant mountains and lush green
symbols.text: Mountains speak of scale and endurance. The lush green beneath them signals earth element at full strength: fertility, solid ground, potential that is already rooted.

ace-of-pentacles.upright: Something you built has materialized. The Ace does not announce the arrival of random good fortune — it marks the moment when careful work solidifies into something you can actually hold. This is the card of the first real payment, the first real client, the first real proof. Spend it wisely but spend it. Money that does not move does not grow.
ace-of-pentacles.reversed: The reward is delayed, diminished, or caught in paperwork. Reversed, the Ace suggests effort that has not yet converted into matter, or matter that is tied up somewhere you cannot access it. Check whether you are waiting for permission you do not need, or whether the deal itself has stalled.
ace-of-pentacles.love: A commitment that becomes concrete — meeting the family, moving in, the moment when feeling converts into shared life.
ace-of-pentacles.work: A raise, a promotion, a contract signed, or the first real income from something you built. The work has assembled into proof.
ace-of-pentacles.sajuLens: The Ace speaks directly to 土(earth), the element of material form and accumulation. For 일간 with earth stems — 戊(Wu) or 己(Ji) — this card often reads as validation: you work in the currency the card is counting in, and this is simply result following method. For 水(water) Day Masters, who navigate flow and adaptation, the Ace can feel slightly rigid, too fixed in form; the reward is real but it may bind you to something stationary. For 火(fire) charts, which burn through resources and move quickly, the Ace warns: hold this carefully, or it will disappear as fast as it arrived. 木(wood) charts tend to see it as a checkpoint before the next expansion. 金(metal) respects its precision and edge.

two-of-pentacles.title: Two of Pentacles
two-of-pentacles.summary: The Two of Pentacles shows a juggler dancing between competing demands — coins, ships, storms. It is the card of skillful adaptation, where the real work is staying in motion.
meaning: The Two of Pentacles is a card of deliberate imbalance. The juggler does not solve the problem by making the coins stop moving or the sea calm down. He solves it by moving faster, by staying alert, by treating the endless switching of attention as its own form of grace. In the KSaju deck he is a street performer in patchwork hanbok, which is to say someone without fixed station — exactly the person who has learned to thrive in circumstances that would paralyze someone rooted to a single method.

The infinity serpent linking the two coins suggests that this is not about choosing one thing or the other. It is about understanding that the two are inseparable, that the dance between them never ends, and that this is the point. The card appears when you have stopped waiting for balance to arrive and started using it as a verb instead — a continuous choice, renewed each moment, to keep both things in the air.

symbols.label: The two glowing brass yeopjeon coins
symbols.text: Yeopjeon were real Joseon currency, but here they are weightless and luminous — not the problem itself but its symbol. The card is not about money, it is about any two things that demand your focus at once and refuse to be serialized into a queue.

symbols.label: The infinity serpent
symbols.text: It connects the coins in a loop that has no beginning and no end. This is not a temporary arrangement you are enduring until you can settle on one thing. The card suggests the linking itself is permanent, and the skill lies in choreographing the dance rather than escaping it.

symbols.label: The merchant ships in the stormy sea
symbols.text: Two vessels navigating enormous waves in the background. They show what happens when you stop juggling — when you commit to one course and the circumstances shift anyway. The juggler's dance is actually the more stable position.

symbols.label: The colorful patchwork hanbok and effortless grace
symbols.text: The clothes are made of scraps, not woven from whole cloth. The juggler belongs nowhere and everywhere — his patchwork is not a sign of poverty but of adaptability. The grace matters more than the costume.

two-of-pentacles.upright: You are managing two legitimate claims on your attention and there is no resolution that gives either one what it wants. The card says: stop looking for the resolution. Treat both as real, stay light on your feet, and accept that the work is the continuous adjustment rather than a final settlement. The skill being rewarded here is not effort but rhythm — knowing when to switch, when to pause, when to let momentum carry you through a gap.
two-of-pentacles.reversed: The juggler has dropped one of the coins or the waves have grown too large for the ships to navigate. Reversed, the card suggests that the dance has tipped into chaos, usually because something is still being treated as though it can wait or because you have somehow forgotten that both things actually need attention. Check whether one of the competing demands has simply been abandoned, or whether you are still pretending they can be balanced when the conditions no longer allow it.
two-of-pentacles.love: Divided attention is the actual condition — stay honest about it instead of pretending you can fake presence.
two-of-pentacles.work: Managing two projects or two versions of the same work that both have to move forward. Your job is the switching, not choosing.
two-of-pentacles.sajuLens: The Two of Pentacles reads through the lens of 土(earth), but its real DNA is movement — the continuous recalibration that keeps the system stable. For a 木 (wood) Day Master, this card often describes life as it naturally occurs: growth requires branching, multiple directions, constant adjustment. For 金 (metal), which prefers singular form and decided shape, the Two of Pentacles reads as a reminder that some seasons demand flexibility even from someone built for structure. For 火 (fire), the inherent drama and audience-awareness of juggling resonates — this is performance-in-real-time. 水 (water) Day Masters usually read this as their native element; the flowing between states is how they already work.

three-of-pentacles.title: Three of Pentacles
three-of-pentacles.summary: Three of Pentacles shows skill being recognized and put to use. Competence meets opportunity. What it means upright, reversed, and through a saju lens.
meaning: The Three of Pentacles is where effort stops being private and becomes visible. A craftsman consults blueprints with a nobleman and a monk — the work is no longer solitary, and it is no longer theoretical. Three yeopjeon are carved into the stone arch above them: the tangible proof that hands and knowledge have produced something real. This is the card of the moment when you are no longer proving yourself in isolation. Someone is watching. Someone approves.

What matters here is not the idea but the execution. The scroll exists, yes, but the stone has already been shaped. The three figures are oriented toward the work itself, not toward each other — cooperation in this card is directed outward, toward the object that requires all of them. This is what distinguishes it from the easier collaborations: no one is here because they like each other. They are here because the task is difficult enough to require more than one kind of expertise.

symbols.label: The craftsman with chisel
symbols.text: His hands are the centre of the image. The work is not an idea he is explaining or a theory he is presenting — it is stone being actively shaped by skill applied in the present tense. Expertise is being performed, not discussed.

symbols.label: The scroll of blueprints
symbols.text: The plan exists, but it is consulted, not followed blindly. The craftsman is not executing orders handed down from above — he is in conversation with the design, showing how it translates into the actual stone in front of him.

symbols.label: The three yeopjeon carved into the arch
symbols.text: Three coins, three people, three kinds of authority: the worker, the patron, the institution. The coins are not payment yet — they are the structure holding everything in place. Competence has been recognized and is now embedded in the work itself.

symbols.label: Warm stone ochre and deep blue robes
symbols.text: The colours ground the scene in real material. This is not a metaphorical collaboration happening in the clouds. The stone is solid, the robes are heavy fabric. The work is tangible and so is the recognition.

three-of-pentacles.upright: Your competence has been noticed and is now being asked to prove itself in a larger context. This is not the card of the lone genius — it is the card of the skilled person whose skills are now genuinely needed. Show up, listen to what the work is actually asking, and do not mistake collaboration for consensus. You are here because you know something the others do not. Trust that knowledge.
three-of-pentacles.reversed: The collaboration is deteriorating into politics, or your skill is being borrowed to cover someone else's mistakes. Reversed, this card often points to being brought in too late to do the work properly, or to being asked to validate something already decided. Step back and check whether you are being consulted or being used.
three-of-pentacles.love: Mutual recognition — attraction is not enough here; there needs to be something you both respect about how the other works.
three-of-pentacles.work: Your competence is now on display and is being rewarded. Do not apologize for the skill that got you here.
three-of-pentacles.sajuLens: Three of Pentacles reads through the lens of 土(earth) — the element of form, of work made manifest, of potential becoming real. For a 일간 whose foundation is 土 — earth stems like 戊(wu-earth) or 己(ji-earth) — this card often arrives as validation of what you have been building all along. The recognition fits naturally. But for a 水(water) Day Master, whose element dissolves fixed form, this card can feel constraining: the collaborators want commitment and clearly-defined roles, while your nature is to remain fluid. For 金(metal) — which prizes perfection and completion — the card reads as the work being good enough to show, but perhaps not finished enough to satisfy. For 火(fire), it is about ego being directed toward the task rather than toward status. For 木(wood), it is about expansion being held in a structure that gives it meaning.

four-of-pentacles.title: Four of Pentacles
four-of-pentacles.summary: The Four of Pentacles shows a Joseon miser gripping coins with fearful intensity. Security through control, or stagnation through grip — depending on what you are holding and why.
meaning: The Four of Pentacles is the card of someone who has finally stopped running. He has gathered enough to matter and now he is afraid to let any of it move. In the KSaju deck he sits on his chest of coins like a bird on eggs, clutching one coin to his sternum, balancing another on his head, standing planted on two more — a posture so rigid it reads as paralysis. Behind him a Joseon city moves and trades and lives without him. He has chosen the safety of holding still.

What makes this card ambiguous is that the choice itself is real. There is nothing wrong with deciding that a particular thing — a position, a relationship, a practice, money — is worth defending rather than expanding. The question the Four asks is whether your grip has become smaller than what you are gripping. Whether you are still choosing security or whether security has chosen you and you are simply too afraid to test whether you could let go.

symbols.label: One coin clutched to the chest
symbols.text: The central coin is held with both hands against the body, held the way you hold something you believe can be stolen. This is not possession — it is anxiety made visible. The tightness of the grip reveals what the card is really about.

symbols.label: One coin balanced on the head
symbols.text: An unstable, precarious position. Even as he grips, he is aware that balance can fail. The coin on top is the one that keeps him vigilant, the vulnerability he cannot quite eliminate no matter how much he holds.

symbols.label: Two coins underfoot
symbols.text: He stands planted on solid ground, but that ground is what he is hoarding. His own stability depends on never moving, on remaining exactly where the coins are. Weight and fixedness are the same thing here.

symbols.label: The bustling city ignored behind him
symbols.text: Market, movement, other people making and trading. He has turned his back on circulation itself. The world does not stop moving because he has stopped — it simply moves without him.

four-of-pentacles.upright: You have something worth keeping and you are keeping it well — for now. The card reads as competence when you are in a genuinely vulnerable position: a young business protecting its margins, a new relationship not yet sturdy enough to soften the boundaries. But watch for the moment when the grip stops being a strategy and becomes a habit. When holding still becomes the only thing you know how to do.
four-of-pentacles.reversed: The grip is failing or the thing being gripped has become worthless. Either you have held so tightly that it is breaking, or circumstances have shifted and you are clutching at something that no longer matters. Release is coming whether you choose it or not.
four-of-pentacles.love: Holding a person this tightly usually means you are more afraid of loss than you are confident in what you have.
four-of-pentacles.work: Protecting what you have built, but at the cost of growth. Useful in a crisis; dangerous as a permanent strategy.
four-of-pentacles.sajuLens: The Four of Pentacles reads through 土(earth) — the element of holding, of boundaries, of keeping things in their place. Earth is necessary for security; earth is also what a prison is made from. If your 일간 is 土, this card often shows up as permission to stabilize — you already understand the grammar of protection and holding firm. If your Day Master runs 木(wood) — the impulse to expand, to break ground, to grow outward — this card warns you that something in your life has calcified. The rigidity that feels like safety to an earth Day Master reads to a wood chart as a cage. The two elements see the same coins and choose opposite interpretations.

five-of-pentacles.title: Five of Pentacles
five-of-pentacles.summary: Five of Pentacles shows hardship at the threshold of help — two beggars in snow pass a lit window they refuse to see. Lingering pride, material loss, and the cost of not looking up.
meaning: The Five of Pentacles is a card about the moment after the fall, when you are still too dizzy to notice that rescue is already visible. Two figures in tattered robes move through deep snow, heads down, bodies bent against cold that has already taken everything portable. Above them burns a merchant's window — warm light, five glowing coins, the whole apparatus of comfort — but neither looks up. The card is not about the cold or the coins. It is about the space between them, the refusal.

What makes this card particular is that help is not absent; it is ignored. This is not abandonment but a kind of blindness that arrives after shame. The beggars have learned to keep their eyes lowered. They have accepted the cold as permanent. What the Five of Pentacles asks is whether you are still moving forward because you believe in forward, or whether you are moving because stopping would mean admitting that the lit window exists and is not for you.

symbols.label: Two figures in Joseon rags
symbols.text: Their clothing is not decoration — it reads as the specific texture of poverty in a particular time and place. They are not suffering generally; they are suffering this, now, in snow that falls on the Korean peninsula, past a tile-roofed house that belongs to the merchant class they will never enter.

symbols.label: Blinding snow, blue-white
symbols.text: The cold is total and visible. It erases the ground beneath their feet and the sky above. Snow in this card is not beautiful or clarifying — it is the thing that makes the warm window above them feel like a hallucination rather than a fact.

symbols.label: Five glowing yeopjeon in the window
symbols.text: The coins glow amber against the snow, warm and deliberate. They are not hidden or hoarded — they sit in the lantern light where anyone could see them. The problem is not that they are inaccessible. The problem is that the beggars have stopped looking.

symbols.label: The brightly lit tile roof
symbols.text: This is not a palace or a temple. It is a merchant's house — the domain of accumulated, ordinary wealth. It represents a kind of prosperity that is theoretically available to anyone willing to engage with trade and material life. The beggars pass it anyway.

five-of-pentacles.upright: You are standing in the cold while help is lit up directly above you. The Five of Pentacles upright is about material difficulty that feels permanent because you have stopped testing whether it actually is. Look up. Not because optimism is a strategy, but because the window is real and your refusal to see it is a choice you are making on top of your circumstances. The card suggests that pride is still costing you more than the cold.
five-of-pentacles.reversed: Reversed, the card shows the moment you finally look up — or the moment someone else forces you to. It can mean accepting help, admitting need, or simply deciding that staying warm matters more than staying dignified. It can also mean the help disappears because you took too long deciding whether to reach for it.
five-of-pentacles.love: Hardship that reveals who is actually looking at you, and who has turned away.
five-of-pentacles.work: A role or project that has stopped paying. Before you freeze in place, decide whether you are waiting for conditions to change or waiting for permission to leave.
five-of-pentacles.sajuLens: The Five of Pentacles sits in 土(earth) — the element of holding, stability, the ground beneath things. Earth people understand material loss acutely because material reality is not abstract to them; it is the foundation they build on. For an 土 Day Master, this card often reads as a necessary reckoning: your ability to survive hardship is real, but your refusal to ask for help is not strength, it is stubbornness. For 火(fire) or 木(wood) Day Masters, the card hits differently — it points to idealism that costs too much, plans that burned through resources without checking if anyone was still paying. For 金(metal) Day Masters, the lit window can feel like a trap: help always comes with conditions and obligation. The card asks what you are protecting by staying cold.

six-of-pentacles.title: Six of Pentacles
six-of-pentacles.summary: The Six of Pentacles shows a merchant balancing generosity with fairness—a moment when abundance flows both ways. What it means upright, reversed, and through a saju lens.
meaning: The Six of Pentacles is the card of someone who has enough and knows it. A Joseon merchant in fine silk stands at the pivot point between having and giving, holding brass scales in one hand—the tool of honest measure—while coins flow from the other. This is not charity performed from a distance. Both parties are present, both are visible, and the transaction is witnessed by the scales themselves. The card describes a state where surplus has become a responsibility, and responsibility has become almost effortless.

What makes this card distinct from simple generosity is the presence of the scales. They suggest that the giver is thinking about fairness, not about performing virtue. The coins are distributed to those who kneel, but the scales ensure no one receives less than their portion or more than they can carry. This is exchange with integrity baked in—the moment when abundance becomes sustainable because it moves in both directions, even if the direction is not yet obvious.

symbols.label: The brass scales
symbols.text: Held steady in one hand, they are the card's centre. Not decorative—actively in use. They measure what is given and ensure balance. The merchant is not guessing at fairness; he is calibrating it.

symbols.label: The silk robes
symbols.text: Fine weave, well-dyed, expensive. The giver is visibly prosperous. There is no performance of sacrifice here—no threadbare cloth to make the giving seem noble. He is wealthy enough that this costs him nothing he will miss.

symbols.label: The yeopjeon coins gleaming in his palm
symbols.text: Three more are visible, ready. The impression is of abundance so present it is almost careless—more coins waiting than the moment requires. This is what surplus actually looks like, not scarcity repackaged as generosity.

symbols.label: The amber and warm brown light
symbols.text: The colour of prosperity, of markets at mid-morning when trade is flowing. Not the white light of charity or the blue-grey of struggle. The entire scene is bathed in the warmth of a functioning economy.

six-of-pentacles.upright: The Six of Pentacles describes a moment when you have more than enough and the abundance is moving. This is not the time to hoard or to perform scarcity. Give what you can afford to give, measure it fairly, and trust that the transaction builds rather than depletes. The scales remind you that fairness matters more than generosity—overgive and you create debt instead of goodwill. This card often appears when partnership, mentorship, or simple exchange is about to deepen.
six-of-pentacles.reversed: The scales tip. Either the giver is depleting themselves—giving from depletion instead of surplus—or the measure has become unfair and one party is carrying the weight. Reversed, this card asks whether you are still operating from abundance or whether you have slipped into the performance of abundance while the actual reserves drain. Check the transaction. Check the scales.
six-of-pentacles.love: An exchange of care that feels balanced and warm—neither person is keeping score, but neither is erasing themselves either.
six-of-pentacles.work: A partnership where skill and resource move in both directions, or a moment to mentor someone without losing yourself in their development.
six-of-pentacles.sajuLens: The Six of Pentacles sits in 土(earth), the element of stability and measurable value. For a 土 Day Master—someone whose chart carries earth as its core—this card usually reads as straightforward; you understand how to measure and distribute fairly because that is how you naturally think. 木(wood) Day Masters often struggle with it; the scales feel like a constraint on spontaneous giving, and the card arrives to remind them that fairness is not the enemy of generosity. 金(metal) Day Masters read this as validation—the scales are precisely their language. 火(fire) and 水(water) Day Masters feel the tension differently: fire gives from inspiration and burns bright but brief, while water flows where it must. For both, the card suggests that lasting abundance requires the merchant's steadiness, not just their heart.

seven-of-pentacles.title: Seven of Pentacles
seven-of-pentacles.summary: The Seven of Pentacles asks whether the work you invested has grown into what you hoped. A Joseon farmer assesses his labor—and his doubts.
meaning: A farmer has tended his ginseng plot with care. Seven coins grow golden among the leaves like fruit he has cultivated. But he leans on his hoe and looks at what he has made, and his expression is not satisfied. This is the card of effort that has produced results without producing joy—the moment when you must decide whether to keep digging or stop.

The Seven does not ask whether you worked hard. It asks whether you are working toward something you actually want. The coins are real. The labor is real. The doubt is also real. When this card appears, you are being invited to reassess: to look at what you have grown and ask whether the yield justifies the soil, whether you should aim differently, invest elsewhere, or simply accept that some crops take longer than you thought to become food.

symbols.label: The hoe, gripped and planted
symbols.text: It is not abandoned but it is not moving. The farmer is paused mid-labor, holding the tool as a prop for thought rather than as an instrument. This is the stance of someone who has stopped to wonder whether the next stroke is worth making.

symbols.label: Seven golden coins among ginseng leaves
symbols.text: Coins do not grow like fruit, but here they do—the literal manifestation of invested time becoming tangible yield. Their gold color marks them as real value, earned. Yet they grow among the plants rather than replacing them, as though the harvest is not quite complete or not quite enough.

symbols.label: One coin resting at his feet
symbols.text: It has either fallen or been set down. Whether this marks a loss, a separation from the yield, or a moment of rest on the work is ambiguous—exactly as ambiguous as the farmer's own doubt about what he is doing.

symbols.label: Deep green and warm gold dusk light
symbols.text: The light is fading. The earthen greens of growth are visible but cooling. The scene holds both ripeness and the sense that seasons change, that the window to decide about this crop is narrowing.

seven-of-pentacles.upright: You have worked. The work has produced something. But you are standing at the moment when effort meets reality and wondering if they align. This is not failure—failure would be easier to read. This is the card of lingering dissatisfaction: you got what you aimed at and discovered you had aimed too low, or you aimed at the wrong target entirely. Before you plant the next row, decide whether you are staying in this field.
seven-of-pentacles.reversed: The doubt has become paralysis. Reversed, the Seven often describes someone who has stopped assessing and started self-sabotaging, or who has decided the work was wasted before giving the yield time to ripen. It can also mark the moment when you walk away from something that was actually working, just because you got tired of waiting for the evidence.
seven-of-pentacles.love: You have built something real. The question is whether it is the thing you actually wanted to build.
seven-of-pentacles.work: Your effort has concrete results. They are simply not matching the vision you had when you started. Time to revise the vision or revise the path.
seven-of-pentacles.sajuLens: The Seven of Pentacles is a 土(earth) card, and earth is the element of harvest, of results made visible and material. For a 土 Day Master, this card often arrives as simple realism: an earth-native typically does not expect satisfaction on the first yield and reads this card as ordinary reassessment. For a 火(fire) native, who tends to move toward what excites rather than what compounds, the Seven can sting—it shows exactly the kind of slow-building effort that fire finds tedious. A 木(wood) Day Master may interpret the farmer's pause as hesitation rather than wisdom and feel pressure to expand rather than refine. 金(metal) natives often read this card clearly: the form is not efficient enough; rebuild. 水(water) natives feel the ambiguity most acutely and may second-guess whether the whole direction is correct.

eight-of-pentacles.title: Eight of Pentacles
eight-of-pentacles.summary: The Eight of Pentacles shows a craftsman perfecting his skill through careful, repetitive work. What it means upright, reversed, and through a saju lens.
meaning: This is the card of the apprentice who has stopped being one. The Joseon craftsman at his workbench is no longer learning the basics — he is refining them, etching each coin with the same precision as the last, building a muscle memory so deep it becomes instinct. Eight coins already hang on the wall. The work is not novel anymore. It is just necessary, and he is good at it precisely because he has stopped expecting it to be anything else.

The Eight of Pentacles measures skill as accumulated repetition. It does not promise inspiration or breakthrough. It promises that if you show up and do the small thing correctly eight times, you will do it correctly the ninth time without thinking. The card appears when discipline has stopped feeling like effort and started feeling like rhythm. This is mastery before it looks like mastery — before anyone else notices.

symbols.label: Eight coins on the wall
symbols.text: Each one finished, each one identical in its precision. The repetition is the entire point. They hang as evidence: this many times, done right. Mastery is not one perfect attempt — it is eight perfect attempts, then nine, then ninety.

symbols.label: The craftsman seated, focused
symbols.text: His posture is steady. He is not straining or inspired. The tool in his hand moves with the ease of something he has done thousands of times. This is what diligence looks like when it has stopped being aspirational.

symbols.label: Master tools, laid out with precision
symbols.text: Everything in its place. The tools themselves are in service to the work, not the other way around. A workspace organized like this is the external version of an organized mind.

symbols.label: Distant town, chosen solitude
symbols.text: He is working apart from the wider world, not because he is isolated but because deep focus requires it. The town exists and he is not in it — that is the choice.

eight-of-pentacles.upright: This is the card of the second month of anything, when the initial excitement has worn off and you are simply showing up. The Eight of Pentacles does not reward ambition — it rewards consistency. Do the same thing correctly, over and over, until your hands know it without asking your mind. Notice that the craftsman is not thinking about becoming a master; he is thinking about the coin in front of him. Mastery arrives as a side effect of that focus.
eight-of-pentacles.reversed: The work has become mechanical without becoming good. You are going through the motions without the focus that makes repetition into skill. Either you have lost the patience the card requires, or the skill you are practicing is not one you actually want to perfect. Reversed, the Eight asks whether you are building something or simply passing time.
eight-of-pentacles.love: Steady, unglamorous care for the relationship itself — the daily choice to show up and do it right.
eight-of-pentacles.work: Competence built through unglamorous repetition. You are ready for the work that requires craftsmanship, not inspiration.
eight-of-pentacles.sajuLens: The Eight of Pentacles is 土(earth) work — patient accumulation, the building of something solid and visible, layer by layer. For someone whose 일간 (Day Master) is 土, this card often reads as simple description: this is how you work naturally, how you build, how you gain confidence. But for a 火(fire) Day Master, whose energy moves in bursts and arcs toward novelty, the Eight of Pentacles can feel like confinement — a card warning that your next leap requires this foundation first. For 金(metal), which also values precision, the Eight reads as permission to be boring in service of excellence. For 水(water), whose nature is changeable, this card pulls you toward the discipline that stops things falling apart.

nine-of-pentacles.title: Nine of Pentacles
nine-of-pentacles.summary: The Nine of Pentacles shows a woman alone in her garden at the height of prosperity — not through inheritance or luck, but through her own sustained effort. Material security earned.
meaning: This is the card of someone who has built something and now lives inside it without anxiety. The Joseon noblewoman in the garden is not waiting for permission or approval; she moves through her own space with the particular ease of someone who knows exactly what she has and how she got it. The nine yeopjeon glowing among the vines are not abstract wealth — they are the tally of compounded good decisions, each one small, each one deliberate.

What matters here is the solitude. She is not showing off for an audience. She is not entertaining anyone or managing anyone else's comfort. The falcon on her glove is trained to her hand alone. This is the card of independence that comes through mastery: you are free not because you refused constraint, but because you learned to work inside it so thoroughly that the constraint dissolved.

symbols.label: The woman alone in the garden
symbols.text: She is not isolated — she is solitary by choice. The garden is hers, which means she can afford to be the only person in it. Solitude reads as luxury when it is voluntary.

symbols.label: The trained falcon on her gloved hand
symbols.text: A bird trained requires years of patient work and intimate knowledge. It obeys her not through coercion but through the precision of her handling. It is a symbol of mastery, not dominion.

symbols.label: Nine yeopjeon glowing on the vines
symbols.text: Nine is the number just before completion. The yeopjeon themselves are real currency, not metaphor. Abundance here is material, specific, and earned through accumulation rather than luck.

symbols.label: Fruit trees and flowering plants at golden hour
symbols.text: The garden is in its season of ripeness and yield. Golden light marks a moment of harvest — not the frantic picking, but the pause after, when you can finally admire what grew.

nine-of-pentacles.upright: You are where you wanted to be and you got there through your own hands. The Nine of Pentacles reads as earned security — the kind that holds because it rests on a foundation you built yourself. Expect this card to show up when the work has finally become sustainable, when the systems you put in place are now running without your constant intervention. The ease you are feeling is real and it is yours to keep.
nine-of-pentacles.reversed: The garden is beautiful but you are not sure you deserve to be in it. Reversed, this card often points to security that feels precarious despite being solid, or to independence that costs you more than you want to admit. Check whether you are actually resting or simply performing rest.
nine-of-pentacles.love: Comfortable alone. If you are with someone, it is because you chose them, not because you needed them.
nine-of-pentacles.work: Mastery that looks effortless because the effort is behind you. You have earned the authority to move at your own pace.
nine-of-pentacles.sajuLens: The Nine of Pentacles sits in 土(earth) — the element of accumulation, stability, the harvest gathered in. For a 土 Day Master, this card reads as home language: you already think in terms of tangible yield and patient building. For a 木(wood) chart, the card can feel restrictive — all that careful tending and no room to expand. A 火(fire) Day Master may find the solitude uncomfortable; they read this as isolation rather than independence. 金(metal) charts resonate with the precision required; 水(water) charts sense the stillness and may wonder whether there is enough movement left in the picture.

ten-of-pentacles.title: Ten of Pentacles
ten-of-pentacles.summary: The Ten of Pentacles is earned rest — three generations gathered under a roof they built together, with ten coins forming an arch overhead. What it means upright, reversed, and through a saju lens.
meaning: The Ten of Pentacles is where the suit of earth settles into its final form: not wealth as accumulation, but wealth as continuity. In the KSaju deck, a Joseon family spans three generations in a tiled courtyard, and the ten yeopjeon coins hang above them like a promise kept. This is the card that answers the question 'what is all this for?' — the answer being lineage, stability proven across time, the kind of security that does not vanish in one generation.

Upright, the card describes inheritance in its widest sense: property, yes, but also method, tradition, the weight of doing things a certain way because they have worked. The dogs at the elder's feet suggest animals cared for long-term, land occupied long-term, the slow accumulation of small loyalties that add up to a life. This is prosperity that has learned to sit still and watch what it built.

symbols.label: Ten yeopjeon coins in an arch
symbols.text: The coins form a gateway rather than a wall, open overhead like a blessing. They are not locked away but distributed — the shape suggests abundance that has learned to circulate without scattering. An arch is stronger than any individual stone.

symbols.label: Three generations gathered
symbols.text: Elder in formal robes seated at the center, a couple with child nearby. The vertical stacking of time is visible: the card is not about one person's success but about what survives the handoff from one pair of hands to the next.

symbols.label: The grand tile-roofed estate
symbols.text: Specific architecture, specific climate, specific permanence. This is not portable wealth but rooted wealth — land that knows your family's name, buildings that will outlast whoever currently inhabits them.

symbols.label: Ochre and deep blue
symbols.text: Warm earth tones grounded by the cooler blue. The palette itself suggests something that has settled: fire burned down to embers, sky at dusk rather than high noon. This is prosperity that has learned to breathe.

ten-of-pentacles.upright: What you have built is old enough now to pass on. The card suggests that stability has compounded into something worth protecting — not obsessively, but with the care you would give to something that will outlive you. If you have no inheritors yet, the card often points to the systems and habits you are encoding that others will eventually adopt without being asked. This is the card of the founder who becomes invisible because their methods became the normal way.
ten-of-pentacles.reversed: The inheritance arrives broken, or the security was always thinner than it looked. Reversed, the Ten of Pentacles often points to wealth that cannot be handed down — squandered by the generation after, or built on something that will not survive scrutiny. Sometimes it signals the person who has wealth but refuses to let it move, choking it to death with control.
ten-of-pentacles.love: The kind of partnership that builds something that lasts — not passion, but the slow compounding of ordinary choices repeated well.
ten-of-pentacles.work: A legacy position, or the chance to build something that will outlive your tenure. You are not being asked to innovate but to solidify.
ten-of-pentacles.sajuLens: The Ten of Pentacles is 土(earth) fully settled, the element that represents stability, harvest, the long view. For a 日干 (Day Master) that is itself 土 — earth, someone whose chart already understands gathering and holding — this card reads almost as autobiography, the natural end of what earth energy builds. But for a 火 (fire) Day Master, whose nature is to burn through, to move on, to shed skin: this card arrives differently. It is not describing your native velocity; it is showing you the foundation someone else's fire will rest on, and asking whether you can build without needing to see the flames.

page-of-pentacles.title: Page of Pentacles
page-of-pentacles.summary: The Page of Pentacles is a student holding a single coin, learning to see value in material things. What it means upright, reversed, and through a saju lens.
meaning: The Page of Pentacles is a Joseon scholar in a field of new green wheat, studying a single yeopjeon coin as though it contains language. This is not greed — it is the posture of someone discovering that the physical world has grammar, that attention to small material things is itself a form of knowledge. He stands at the threshold where curiosity becomes discipline, where play becomes practice.

What arrives with this card is the appetite to build something that will hold its shape. Unlike the major arcana pages, who are often caught in motion, the Page of Pentacles is still — not frozen but focused. He has chosen what to study. The card suggests a long apprenticeship beginning, or a foundation being laid so carefully that it seems almost boring until suddenly you notice how solid it has become.

symbols.label: The single yeopjeon coin
symbols.text: One coin, studied intently at eye level. Not pocketed, not spent — examined. The coin represents value itself as something learnable, something that has to be understood before it can be used properly. This is the card of someone teaching themselves to read a language they had not known was written.

symbols.label: Fresh green wheat
symbols.text: New growth, practical and rooted. The field is not decorative; it establishes that value is not abstract but grows from soil and season and labour. The Page stands in the evidence of growth that takes time to show its results.

symbols.label: Mountains in the background
symbols.text: Distant and steady. They frame the scene without dominating it, suggesting both the scale of what could be learned and the fact that the Page is beginning where he is, not waiting to climb first.

symbols.label: Spring light and warm gold
symbols.text: The season and the metal of the coin echo each other. This is new energy put into material practice — enthusiasm for learning something real, something that has weight and consequence.

page-of-pentacles.upright: Something practical is beginning to make sense to you, or you are beginning to make sense of something practical. The Page of Pentacles moves slowly but with genuine focus; he does not skip steps because skipping teaches nothing. If this card arrives, a foundation is worth building properly. Commit to the unglamorous work of learning the details — they will compound.
page-of-pentacles.reversed: Either the study has not begun despite the intention, or it has become rote and lifeless, all form and no discovery. Reversed, the Page suggests either distraction from a commitment that was real, or the habit of looking busy while nothing actually settles into your hands. Check whether you are still curious or merely dutiful.
page-of-pentacles.love: Early attention, someone still learning who you are. It reads as tender and provisional both.
page-of-pentacles.work: Apprenticeship, mastery starting from zero, or the unglamorous phase before competence shows. Build well now.
page-of-pentacles.sajuLens: Earth 土 is the element of gathering, of making something tangible from scattered potential — the saju equivalent of what the Page of Pentacles holds. If your 일간 is 土, this card often simply confirms the pace you already work at: careful, sequential, willing to seem slow because you are building to last. If your Day Master is 火 — fire, which moves fast and wants visibility — the Page reads as a necessary friction, a reminder that some things cannot be rushed. If you are 水 — water, fluid and adaptive, the Page points toward the structure that feels constraining but makes your work finally hold its shape.

knight-of-pentacles.title: Knight of Pentacles
knight-of-pentacles.summary: The Knight of Pentacles is steady labour made visible — a cavalry officer who examines one coin with the same care most give to empires. What it means upright, reversed, and through a saju lens.
meaning: The Knight of Pentacles is the only knight in the deck who is not in motion. His horse stands completely still in a ploughed field, and his attention is fixed on a single yeopjeon held in his hand. He is a Joseon cavalry officer, which means he has training, discipline, and the weight of responsibility — but what he demonstrates is not the use of those things. He demonstrates patience. The card is about work that does not announce itself, about the kind of reliability that shows up the same way every morning.

This is not the card of ambition or of visible progress. It is the card of someone tending what is already there: examining the ground before ploughing it again, holding one coin long enough to really see it, knowing that the oak tree behind him took decades to grow and will take decades more. When he turns up in a reading he is asking whether you are willing to be bored by your own commitment, whether you can do the same useful thing repeatedly without needing it to transform into something else.

symbols.label: The heavy black shire horse, completely still
symbols.text: Built for pulling, not for speed. The horse is not champing or restless — it simply stands. This is the image of force held in reserve, power that does not need to prove itself by moving.

symbols.label: The single yeopjeon examined with methodical care
symbols.text: One coin, not a handful. The Knight is not assessing wealth or counting fortune — he is studying the thing itself, the way a farmer studies soil. The attention itself is the point.

symbols.label: Plain but polished armor
symbols.text: Not ornate, not new. The armor is functional and maintained. It suggests someone who takes care of the tools he uses but does not mistake care for status.

symbols.label: The ploughed field and oak tree
symbols.text: Dark green and earthy brown. Both represent work already done and work that will take years to complete. The field has been broken; the tree was not planted yesterday.

knight-of-pentacles.upright: The Knight of Pentacles shows up when patience has become your job. You are not building something visible yet — you are laying foundation, checking details, doing the work that looks like nothing to anyone watching. This is the card of the apprentice, the farmer before harvest, the person tending something that will not mature on a schedule that suits anyone's impatience. Stay methodical. The results will come slower than you want and that is exactly the speed they need.
knight-of-pentacles.reversed: The patience has curdled into stagnation, or else it was never there to begin with. Reversed, the Knight points either to work that is moving nowhere because something in the foundation was never examined, or to someone grinding through the motions without actually paying attention. Before you assume you are being responsible, check whether you are actually present in what you are doing.
knight-of-pentacles.love: Steady accumulation of small kindnesses over time. Not romance — something quieter and more durable.
knight-of-pentacles.work: Methodical work on something that will not be finished this quarter. Your job is to keep the standard consistent, not to speed it up.
knight-of-pentacles.sajuLens: The Knight of Pentacles runs on 土(earth) — the element of groundedness, harvest, and the slow accumulation that turns effort into something you can hold. If your 일간 is 土, this card reads as a description of how you already move through the world: careful, building value gradually, comfortable with long timescales. If your Day Master is 火(fire), which needs visibility and momentum, the Knight arrives as resistance — a reminder that some things cannot be rushed, that your impatience is not a flaw in the timing but a flaw in your estimate of how long the work actually takes. If you are 水(water), flowing and adaptive, the Knight's stillness can feel like restriction, though what it is actually offering is the ballast that keeps you from being swept away by every current.

queen-of-pentacles.title: Queen of Pentacles
queen-of-pentacles.summary: The Queen of Pentacles is settled devotion made visible — a woman whose strength is in what she tends, not what she claims. What it means upright, reversed, and through a saju lens.
meaning: The Queen of Pentacles is the card of a woman who has stopped reaching and started rooting. She sits on a throne carved with the marks of abundance — fruit, goat, the evidence of a life that produces — and she holds a single yeopjeon as if it were her child. The card is not about wealth. It is about the kind of attention that turns a coin into something precious, a garden into a reason to wake. She has made peace with staying, and in that peace she has become the thing everyone reaches toward.

What she offers is not excitement but reliability — the warmth of someone who will be exactly where she said she would be, who remembers what you told her, who knows the difference between a problem and a disaster. The flowers and fruits surrounding her are not decoration; they are the language she speaks. In Joseon, the queen was the keeper of the household's continuity. This card describes that role at any scale: the person who holds the center so others can move outward, who measures her power not in conquest but in what she has made stable enough to last.

symbols.label: The yeopjeon cradled in her lap
symbols.text: A single coin held as tenderly as an infant. It is not the amount of money that matters — it is the attention. This is what she does with whatever she has: she looks at it fully, knows its weight, understands its worth. She is teaching the card's reader to do the same.

symbols.label: The stone throne carved with fruit and goat
symbols.text: Fruit speaks to harvest, to cycles that complete themselves. The goat — a creature that tends the land, that produces milk and warmth — is carved into the foundation of her power. She sits on abundance that has already proven itself through work, not through luck.

symbols.label: The rabbit at her feet
symbols.text: Small, alive, unafraid in her presence. The rabbit is quick but it has chosen to stay near her. This is what the Queen of Pentacles creates: a space where living things feel safe enough to be themselves.

symbols.label: The lush garden and distant mountains
symbols.text: Green and gold, earth energy made visible. The mountains are far enough away to be solid — this is not a card of distant dreams but of the actual ground she stands on, every day, tended with real hands.

queen-of-pentacles.upright: This is the card of showing up, of paying attention to what is actually in front of you instead of what you wish were there. The Queen of Pentacles does not inspire with speeches; she inspires by example — by being the person whose yes means yes, whose presence settles things. If this card appears, you are being asked to do what she does: tend something with full focus, let it matter to you, and trust that reliability is its own form of power. She is not glamorous. She is the thing that lasts.
queen-of-pentacles.reversed: The devotion has curdled into resentment, or the settling has become entrapment. Reversed, the Queen of Pentacles suggests someone who has tended so consistently that they have forgotten they had a choice, or who is offering care to someone who has stopped recognizing it as gift. The card warns: check whether you are still rooting or merely stuck. Taking care of yourself is not the same as being selfish.
queen-of-pentacles.love: A love that has moved past intensity into actual presence — someone who knows your real self and chooses to stay.
queen-of-pentacles.work: Mastery of the small, reliable details. You are being asked to be the one people know they can trust to follow through.
queen-of-pentacles.sajuLens: The Queen of Pentacles carries 土 (earth) — the element of stability, harvest, the holding center. Earth is what receives seed and transforms it into growth; it is the 일간 that leans toward grounding and completing what has been begun. If your Day Master is earth, this card often reads as permission to stop proving yourself and start building — you are already built to do this. If your Day Master is 水 (water), which seeks flow and adaptation, the Queen's stillness may feel restrictive; she is asking you whether you can find groundedness without losing responsiveness. For 木 (wood) — expansion — she offers a different question: is what you are building worth staying for? Metal 金 and fire 火 Day Masters tend to see her as the solution to their own instability: the reminder that power lives in depth, not surface.

king-of-pentacles.title: King of Pentacles
king-of-pentacles.summary: The King of Pentacles is a Joseon merchant-lord who has mastered material abundance and learned to distribute it. What it means upright, reversed, and through a saju lens.
meaning: This is not the card of someone who hoards. The King of Pentacles has built enough that he can afford to let it move — through his hands, through his city, through the people who depend on him. He sits on a throne grown over with grapevines, a plant that produces without demanding constant intervention, and his robe carries both grapes and coins: the harvest and the exchange. He is the endpoint of earth's journey through the suit — not the first coin found, but the man who has learned what coins are actually for.

The scepter he holds is authority, but it is the yeopjeon in his other hand that defines him. He is generous not from sentiment but from the clarity of someone who understands that hoarded wealth is just weight. His city towers rise around him because he knows how to keep things growing. This card appears when abundance has stopped being theoretical and has become something you actually know how to tend.

symbols.label: The throne of grapevines
symbols.text: Grapevines produce reliably and require patience rather than constant intervention. His seat is built from something that renews itself — a material metaphor for sustainable abundance, not extracted wealth that depletes.

symbols.label: Bull carvings on throne and stone
symbols.text: The bull is steady, grounded, capable of bearing weight. It appears both as carving and beneath his foot, grounding his authority in earth itself — this is power that comes from the land, not from conquest.

symbols.label: Robe embroidered with grapes and coins
symbols.text: The distinction between what grows and what is exchanged is stitched directly into his clothing. He is neither merchant nor farmer alone, but someone who understands both the production and the distribution of value.

symbols.label: The city towers surrounding him
symbols.text: Prosperity is visible at scale. His wealth has created infrastructure that others depend on — the card shows not private richness but abundance that has shaped an entire place.

king-of-pentacles.upright: You have built something stable enough that you can stop defending it and start sharing it. The King of Pentacles reads as competence with real weight behind it — not the beginner's luck of the early suit cards, but mastery that has learned to be generous without becoming reckless. This is the card of someone who can give without losing. Hold what you have built to a standard: does it still serve only you, or has it become big enough to serve others?
king-of-pentacles.reversed: The grip has tightened. Reversed, this is either abundance that has turned to hoarding, or competence that has calcified into control. The king still sits on his throne, but the grapevines have stopped producing — everything is now extraction and no circulation. Check whether you are protecting something worth protecting, or just afraid to let it move.
king-of-pentacles.love: A partner who is resourceful and faithful, but whose love expresses itself through provision rather than intensity.
king-of-pentacles.work: Mastery in your domain, and the authority to decide how your skill gets distributed. You have earned the right to say no to projects that do not align.
king-of-pentacles.sajuLens: The King of Pentacles runs on 土(earth) — the element of consolidation, boundaries, the gathering of what has been scattered into something held. For a 土 Day Master, this card often reads as home territory; your instinct for building and tending is what the card is describing, and reversed it suggests you have become too rigid. A 木(wood) Day Master — growth and expansion — often finds this card frustrating; the suit's patience can feel like stalling, and the emphasis on holding steady reads as constraint. For 火(fire), the card's generosity appeals, but the steadiness can seem boring. 金(metal) recognizes the structure immediately. 水(water) may see the abundance as something to flow through rather than be contained by.
